speechtext: That a select committee be appointed to continue the examination of all expenditure of public moneys for national defence and all commitments for expenditure for national defence since March 31, 1950, and to report from time to time their observations and opinions thereon, and in particular, what, if any, economies consistent with the execution of the policy decided by the government may be effected therein, with power to send for persons, papers and records and to examine witnesses; and that notwithstanding standing order 65. the committee shall consist of twenty-six members to be designated by the house at a later date.

speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxton (Minisier of National Defence):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I was away attending the meetings of the North Atlantic treaty council when the Currie report was presented to this house and discussed on December 15, 16 and 17 I feel that it would be the wish of hon. members, and indeed of others throughout the country, in view of the wide interest attached to this important document, that I should take advantage of the first opportunity of dealing with it on the motion to set up this committee and in the course of my remarks to indicate in support of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) the reasons why I believe this report should receive the consideration of that committee, if and when it is set up.
In the debate which took place between December 15 when the Currie report was tabled and the Christmas adjournment on December 17, reference was also made to a number of other matters relating to national defence about which I may have something to say on another occasion. But today I intend to confine what I have to say to the Currie report itself and to matters relevant to it.
Before entering into this subject I should like if I may to make a personal reference. For the affairs of the Department of National Defence and the three armed services of Canada I am responsible under the statute under which I was appointed. I have accepted and have endeavoured to discharge that responsibility to the best of my ability. I have no intention of trying to dodge that responsibility. There has not been and there will not be any effort made to find a scapegoat. When we found that there had been wrongdoing, we laid prosecutions. When it appeared, as I said in the house on April 21, that there had been "grave irregularities", I

Committee on Defence Expenditure appointed Mr. Currie to investigate the causes and to suggest some means to prevent their recurrence.
As he says, in the investigation he was given every facility. He made his report and by the time we had received it action had already been taken which anticipated the majority of his recommendations. The report shows that a good system of accounting had been worked out, approved and adopted, but was not carried fully into effect. No government department, no commercial enterprise, no large-scale undertaking can be perfect. In an operation of the magnitude of the expansion of the defence effort of Canada there are bound to be mistakes, just as by the law of averages there are bound to be some thefts and some fires. We have had these in the past and most certainly we will have them in the future. As I said in the house in 1947:
While much progress has been made, no one appreciates more than myself that there is still a lot of work to be done in reorganization before we can provide a proper organizational and administrative basis for the defence forces that we may have in the future.
Perhaps I have been overenthusiastic in the defence of the armed forces against what I felt to be unjustified charges, and sometimes I may have been overoptimistic; but it is pretty hard to work with the armed forces of Canada without having high admiration for their fine record of achievement and without having faith in their capacity to do what is expected of them.
When things happened which were wrong and when they were brought to my attention I tried to take whatever action appeared to be most likely to put matters right. As long as I have the responsibility of speaking in this house for the armed forces of Canada 1 shall try to deal promptly with wrongdoing and to correct situations that need correction; but I am not going to blame others for shortcomings unless I am satisfied that they are responsible for them.
Some confusion has arisen regarding the handling of the report itself. First of all, let me emphasize, as the Prime Minister and the Solicitor General (Mr. Campney) have done, that there was only one report, and that is the report signed by Mr. Currie himself. He did not make any other report. There was no interim report.
The only report Mr. Currie made was the report he signed. That was given to the deputy minister of national defence on Monday, December 8. Unfortunately, the fact that the signed report was dated November 26 seems to have given rise to some confusion.
LMr. Claxton.l

However, no copy of the signed report was received by the Department of National Defence prior to December 8, 1952.
Here I should point out that throughout this whole investigation Mr. Currie and those associated with him worked closely with the department and the army. Mr. Currie referred to "the ready and full co-operation" accorded to him. I am sure that he would be the first to say that a large part of the information he and his associates received came from the department and the army works services.
As regards the presentation of the report, most of the information I have was given to me by the deputy minister of national defence, Mr. C. M. Drury.
From time to time Mr. Currie's representatives, and on two occasions Mr. Currie himself, discussed with Mr. Drury the form in which the irregularities at Petawawa would be presented in the report. I believe that this was back in September or October. Mr. Davey, an associate of Mr. Currie who had been doing a large part of the investigational work, indicated to Mr. Drury that he proposed to list extracts from the R.C.M.P. files, attributing to the R.C.M.P. the information so given.
Mr. Drury was concerned as to how such information was to be handled, and this for several reasons. Its appearance might be taken to prejudice the criminal or military cases which were still pending. It might damage innocent persons, and it might compromise other police investigations. Mr. Davey showed Mr. Drury a typewritten draft showing the form in which it was proposed to present this information. Mr. Drury pointed out that the publication of R.C.M.P. investigation reports was something that the department had always endeavoured to avoid. These reports were confidential, and if they were not treated as such future police investigations might be hampered. Mr. Davey undertook to have consideration given to changing the form of presentation.
In a later discussion Mr. Davey said that changes had been made and Mr. Drury suggested to Mr. Davey that he might have a look at the revised form of presentation of the irregularities. Mr. Davey said that this was now embodied in the draft of the whole report and it was not Mr. Currie's intention that anyone review the draft before presentation of the report. Mr. Drury reported this conversation to me. I told Mr. Drury that in the interests of Mr. Currie, as well as of the department and the army, it would be desirable that the report should be as factually accurate as possible, and I thought

that he might suggest to Mr. Currie that he let him see a draft of the report to check it for factual errors.
What date was that?

This would be about the 25th or 26th of November. Mr. Currie of course was perfectly free to follow that course or not as he wished. As he himself says in the letter to me of December 29:
On the 26th November, before the checking and final consideration had been completed by me here, Mr. Drury, the deputy minister, called on the telephone from Ottawa. During his telephone conversation with me, Mr. Drury mentioned the minister and went on to intimate to me that it seemed desirable that the final text of the intended report be submitted to him (before the report was actually signed and delivered) in order that purely factual matters dealt with in the report could be verified as to their accuracy. I gathered that his reason for this was that in such connection there had been instances in the Mainguy report where purely factual matters of this nature had not been properly dealt with.
While, during this conversation with Mr. Drury, I expressed some disinclination to follow such a course, the upshot was that it was understood that I would submit to him one of the two print reproduction copies above referred to, but solely for the purpose of enabling verification of factual matters and data dealt with in the report as so formulated. I decided that I would ask my partner, Mr. Cleary, to personally deliver the said copy to the deputy minister. I called Mr. Cleary, who was in Ottawa, and described the situation to him. That afternoon I had one of the two print reproduction copies which I had received from the printer mailed to Mr. Cleary, who, on the following day, the 27th November, delivered it in person to the deputy minister.
On Monday, December 1, Mr. Drury met Mr. Cleary, another of Mr. Currie's associates, and Mr. Davey, as has already been outlined by tne Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). As a result Mr. Currie made some minor changes, signed the report and forwarded it to the deputy minister under cover of the letter dated December 8.
It has been suggested in the house that it was wrong for anyone in the department to look first at the draft of the report, and the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), who is generally very fair, has even suggested in a radio broadcast that Mr. Currie should perhaps be blamed for showing the draft to the deputy minister. I cannot see anything wrong in what was done. I think that the suggestion that it was wrong arises from a misconception of what Mr. Currie was asked to do and what he was doing. Mr. Currie was not carrying on a criminal investigation. That was being done by the R.C.M.P., the army provost corps, and the Department of Justice. Mr. Currie was not investigating the Department of National Defence, and he was not investigating the Minister of National Defence.
Committee on Defence Expenditure
As Minister of National Defence I had asked Mr. Currie to make an investigation for me of the causes of a bad situation which had been found at Petawawa and to recommend to me how that bad situation could be cleared up. I was afraid the bad situation might be more widespread in the army works services, and that is why I asked Mr. Currie to look at that whole branch of the army right across Canada. I wanted the truth and I wanted the kind of report which nobody would question. I did not want errors of fact anywhere in the report which might discredit the whole report and make it more difficult to implement any recommendations it might make to improve the situation.
I am glad, and I am sure the house is glad, that Mr. Currie accepted Mr. Drury's correction and took out the reference to the soldier who had been accused of stealing materials and using army labour to build a cottage because that soldier had already been acquitted in the courts and it would have been unfortunate to have done him the injustice of leaving in that reference. I am sorry the report contained the reference to the Canadian National rails which turned out not to be there, and I am sorry it contained the reference to the horses, though I am glad they were not on the payroll.
At the same time I can understand why Mr. Currie did not consider it necessary to check the irregularities at Petawawa very carefully. He was not carrying on the criminal investigation. He had another job altogether, to find the causes and recommend means of preventing their recurrence. That is what the report is supposed to be about. I am glad, and I know other hon. members are glad, that Mr. Currie found no new evidence of extensive irregularities and that he felt justified in cautioning us not to blame the whole army works services for the conduct of a "handful of crooks".
I still believe that the report would be a better report if these errors of fact I have mentioned, and a number of others, had not been left in it. That was what I wanted to have prevented when I told Mr. Drury that he might suggest to Mr. Currie that a final check be made for errors of fact. Of course it was up to Mr. Currie to decide whether to have that check made, and he did decide to do so, and he did make a few changes. But they were made on his own responsibility, and Mr. Drury did not even know which of them had been made until he received the signed report on December 8.
Like other hon. members, I was astonished to find that another copy of the draft, apparently a duplicate of the copy shown to Mr. Drury,

Committee on Defence Expenditure .had got into the hands of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and had been referred to by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) in the house on December 15. This copy was seen by the Prime Minister and the Solicitor General (Mr. Campney) I believe on the same day. It appeared to be an exact duplicate of the report itself except that in the latter some pages had been reprinted.
The only copy of the draft received by the Department of National Defence was the copy handed to the deputy minister on November 27. That copy was returned to Mr. Currie's representative on December 8 at the same time that the signed report was presented. Consequently the draft in the hands of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre could not have reached him from the Department of National Defence. As the release to unauthorized persons of a draft of a report of this character is a matter of great concern, I wrote Mr. Currie a letter on December 22, 1952, and received from him replies dated December 24 and December 29,
1952.	I wrote Mr. Currie again on January 2,
1953,	and received from him a letter dated January 7, 1953. I also wrote the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre asking if Mr. Currie could see the copy of the draft received from the hon. member for Kosetown-Biggar, and I received a reply dated January 5, 1953. Meanwhile one of Mr. Currie's associates examined the copy of the draft given to the hon. member for Kosetown-Biggar and examination made it plain that this copy was in fact one of the drafts prepared by Mr. Currie's printer. Mr. Currie wrote me to this effect in his letter of January 7, 1953. In the concluding paragraph of that letter Mr. Currie said:
Everything which I have done by way of inquiry and investigation negatives the possibility that the copy in question could have got out in any stage or step between the printer's shop and my own organization and the department; but I still, of course, welcome any further investigation which the department or any other authority may deem it expedient to make from any angle or direction.
Would the minister put that entire exchange of letters into the records?

I would be glad to do so.
While the explanation as to how a copy got into unauthorized hands was the responsibility of Mr. Currie and remains his responsibility, it seemed to me and it seemed to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) that the theft or other improper act by which the copy got into unauthorized hands was of such a general concern that it should be followed up and the R. C. M. P. were accordingly instructed to investigate and report.
(Mr. Claxton.]
Hear, hear.

On January 8 I wrote the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and on January 9 I telegraphed Mr. Currie to that effect. To these messages I received a reply from Mr. Coldwell dated January 10, 1953. If I have leave of the house I would now like to table all of the correspondence to which I have referred. I may say that, whether it was necessary or not, I have asked Mr. Currie and the hon. gentleman if they had any objection and they said they saw none.

Mr. Currie has since been in communication with me about the investigation which is still proceeding and about which it is not possible to make a further report at this time.
During the spring and summer of 1951, the Canadian Provost Corps was engaged in investigations at Petawawa military camp and during the same period, as a result of inspections carried out by the chief auditor and the inspector of quartermaster services, deficiencies were found at Petawawa indicating the need for increased supervision. At that time there was no evidence of any criminal act requiring prosecution.
On October 12, 1951, the anonymous letter referred to in the Currie report was received by the R.C.M.P. at Ottawa. There is nothing unusual about this-as everyone knows, a large proportion of crimes are reported and solved in consequence of tip-offs. The letter was forwarded to headquarters central command on October 16, 1951, and as a result, on October 29, 1951, the R.C.M.P. were requested by the deputy minister of national defence to carry out a complete investigation. This investigation was carried out in conjunction with the Canadian Provost Corps. It was commenced immediately and pushed through as rapidly as possible.

During this period no less than thirty-seven major construction projects were being carried out at Petawawa by employees of twenty-four different contracting firms. Anyone with any experience knows how difficult it is to enforce security over building supplies or the disposal of scrap in those circumstances. To be effective the investigation had to be carried on as secretly as possible. Moreover, as the alleged operations had extended over a considerable period, some officers and -men had been posted to other units and the investigation had to be carried on at a number of different places across Canada, including Halifax, Vancouver and Churchill.
Those investigations indicated that some service officers and men and civilians had conspired together to commit a number of thefts and frauds in connection with the disposal of stores and with other operations going on at the camp. By March 10, 1952, the investigation had proceeded to the stage where prosecutions could be laid. A detailed summary of the reports of the R.C.M.P. and the provost corps was put before me. The thoroughness of the investigation can be judged by the results of the prosecutions and from the fact that neither in the court proceedings nor in the Currie report was any substantial additional information disclosed.
Mr. J. W. Pickup, Q.C., was engaged as special counsel and, on his appointment as Chief Justice of Ontario, he was replaced by another distinguished counsel, Mr. T. N. Phelan, Q.C. Five service personnel and ten civilians were prosecuted in the civil courts. Four service personnel and eight civilians were convicted.
The first prosecution was that of Staff Sergeant Young and it began with his arrest on May 13, 1952. The cases were pressed on with all possible expedition and despite intervention of the two months in the summer when the court did not sit all cases and appeals were disposed of by Monday, December 1, when the last case was dealt with in the military courts.
In addition to giving instructions that prosecutions might be laid, consideration was from day to day being given to the steps that should be taken to follow up disclosures made in the police investigation. The result was my appointment of Mr. Currie to make an investigation and report. In the telegram dated April 21, 1952, which already appears on Hansard of that day, Mr. Currie was asked to determine the causes and make recommendations to prevent a recurrence of the irregularities that occurred at Petawawa. His recommendations are contained in
Committee on Defence Expenditure parts II, III and IV of his report. They contain many constructive recommendations with which I will deal later.
It has been suggested that reading the report from the end rather than from the beginning makes a very different impression. However, most people started, as one would expect, at page 1 and I am afraid that a good many of them stopped when they came to the horses. The first point I want to emphasize is that Mr. Currie says in his report that it was only at Petawawa that extensive irregularities over a long period of time took place. Now, Mr. Currie does not say in his report that he discovered any of the irregularities at Petawawa. Most of the irregularities there had already been discovered and that is the reason Mr. Currie was asked to make his investigation, and, in the words of my telegram, "to determine the causes and make recommendations to prevent a recurrence".
Since most of the irregularities referred to in this part of my report were already known to the department, and steps had been taken to deal with them before the investigation began, it would scarcely be necessary to -mention them at all if they were not referred to in the report-
So far as I can discover the summary of nineteen cases given in the report was largely derived from confidential police reports to which, of course, Mr. Currie had access.
The Prime Minister gave the house on December 17 the information he had received from the deputy minister to the effect that page 7 of the draft had contained a paragraph stating that an army corporal had had a cottage built valued at $1,700 out of army materials and army labour for which no reimbursement had been received, or words to that effect.
Mr. Drury pointed out that this soldier had been already acquitted and consequently, as I have mentioned to the house, that passage in the draft was omitted in the report.
Yesterday the Prime Minister dealt with the question of horses. Now, there are a number of other cases in which the account given by Mr. Currie is not fully in accordance with the facts as they have been established in the course of our further investigation or in the courts. However, there is included among these examples of irregularities one statement about which I think I should say something, and that is the reference to the dam.
As the report has it, "a dam was built on Tucker creek at a cost estimated at some $3,000 or $4,000. Its utility is not clear to me and it was in any event not authorized by
936	HOUSE OF
Committee on Defence Expenditure army headquarters". That is Mr. Currie's reference to this instance in his report. According to the information furnished to me by the chief of the general staff, the dam was built as a training exercise to create a source of water to fight fires. This dam was built on Tucker creek, which is a creek of roughly 15 feet to 20 feet in width, and during the summer it dwindles to a very small trickle. It happens that it runs at the western end of one of the target area ranges where live ammunition may cause fires. The closest other source of water is two and a half miles away. Tucker creek would provide a source of water for fire fighting, provided enough water is stored to permit mobile pumps to be used.
The construction of a dam there was advocated as far back as 1927, and again in 1931-32. Early in 1949 a dam was constructed there out of logs and earth with sand bags, but it washed out during the spring freshets in 1950. The following year, as a training exercise for the pioneers of the Royal Canadian Regiment and to build up a reservoir of water for fire fighting purposes, the area commander, with the approval of the general officer commanding central command at the time, had the dam rebuilt of cement. The cost of materials and civilian labour was about $2,000.
This project involved the restoration of the dam which had been washed out by floods. Now, under the regulations applicable at the time, such projects costing not more than $5,000 could be approved by the area or general officer commanding. That is the information given to me by the chief of the general staff.
These, and other cases mentioned by Mr. Currie, are the kind of thing that could be gone into further by the committee, if that is its desire. In the department, and in the army, we want to see that everything is done that can be done to discipline those who have been at fault, and so far as is humanly possible to prevent a recurrence. If I do not refer to the other cases at Petawawa, I hope that no one is going to say that I think what took place at Petawawa is not serious. After all, I do happen to be the person who, on April 21, informed the house that there were grave irregularities. I was also the one who took the view that the situation required a thorough investigation, who had an investigation made, and who had the result made immediately public.
I now turn to the constructive part of Mr. Currie's report, his recommendations as to what could be done to improve the situation in the army works services. It seems to me, in all fairness, we should put the


report and its recommendations in proper perspective, and relate them to the problems and difficulties which the department, the army and the army works services particularly have encountered since the termination of the second world war-facts which are well known to everyone. I should like also to draw attention to some very important differences between the Department of National Defence and other government departments or indeed the work of the Department of National Defence and any civilian activity. These differences result from our form of government, as well as from the nature of the defence operations. They exist in every democratic country.
In other government departments there is a single line, a straight line of responsibility proceeding from the minister, usually through the deputy minister, to all the employees and agencies of the department. In defence, in addition to this chain of responsibilities on the civilian side, there is also the chain of command and the chain of responsibility on the service side. Since the new defence act came into effect in 1950 the service chief heads his service, and each service chief is responsible to the minister for the control and administration of the service. So far as service operations are concerned, each of the services is under the direct control of the chief of staff, who is responsible to the minister-subject, of course, to the scrutiny- and where required the action-of the deputy minister, particularly in matters of estimates, appropriations, financial control and accounting.
Now, let me point to another fact in the organization of the Canadian army which has some importance. The Canadian army, as is the case in most countries, is divided into corps. There are fourteen in all, and they include armour, infantry, signallers, etc. One of the corps is the Royal Canadian Engineers. The engineers, in turn, have two components, the field units which do the engineering work in the field and the army works services which have to do with accommodation and services at static establishments. The Currie report has, of course, to do with this latter branch, that is the army works services and this branch only.
In 1946, the army works services comprised twenty-nine works companies and detachments. The service was reorganized in 1948 into sixteen works companies comprising thirty-three major works detachments across the country extending ultimately from Newfoundland to Vancouver, north to Whitehorse and the Yukon and into the Northwest Territories and the Arctic. The responsibility of the army works services includes: (a) providing buildings for the active and reserve forces,

whether by way of construction, purchase, lease or the renovation of existing buildings;
(b)	works for defence training and operations;
(c)	custody and care of army lands and buildings; (d) maintenance of buildings, training facilities and utilities; (e) operation of water, sewage and electric plants; (f) fire prevention and fire fighting services; (g) preparation of designs and specifications for buildings and other services; (h) planning of buildings and services required for mobilization; (i) handling of salvage for renovation or disposal-and that for all corps in the Canadian army.
The operations of works services from 1946 on extended to all the property the Canadian army had acquired before or during the second world war. This property was located in every part of Canada, and it was in every kind of condition. The buildings and installations constructed in wartime, which were being retained, were deteriorating rapidly. Most of them were designed to have a life of about five years. The army works services were responsible for the custody and maintenance or the renovation or disposal of all of this property.
An additional responsibility was placed upon the army works services with the decision to create "emergency married quarters", and between 1946 and 1948 a total of 4,500 of these were provided through the army works services. During this time too the Alaska highway was taken over from the United States army and the Royal Canadian Engineers army works services had to assume responsibility for its upkeep. The highway covers a distance of 1,250 miles to be kept open twenty-four hours a day the year round. Many of its bridges and culverts, etc., had to be replaced. For each year from 1946 to 1949 the program for the acquisition, construction and maintenance of army property amounted to approximately $20 million. That is the financial measure of the scope of the operations of the army works services during that period. For 1952-53 the program for the same purposes was in excess of $250 million, or more than ten times as much. The strength in 1949-50 was 806 service personnel and 2,936 civilian personnel and in 1951-52 it was 765 service personnel and 3,334 civilian personnel. Hon. members will observe how the civilian personnel outnumbered the service personnel in both years by three to one, or more. With this relatively small increase in personnel the army works services had to carry on the following operations:
(1)	Continue their ordinary peacetime activities of maintaining existing active and reserve buildings and services;
(2)	Continue to handle large stocks of surplus from the second world war;
Committee on Defence Expenditure
(3)	Supply personnel for the 25th brigade in Korea and the 27th brigade in Germany;
(4)	Provide services to meet the additional needs of the army due to its increase from the figure of 20,300 before Korea to a figure of 49,800 two years later;
(5)	Provide training facilities; and
(6)	Have to do with the addition of buildings and permanent services such as roads, sewers, lights, etc., totalling in contracts placed or works undertaken, in the two calendar years subsequent to Korea, the sum of $125,283,905. This amount was represented in no less than 285 different construction contracts, and an estimated 4,100 additional projects involving a total of 7,268 buildings. Heavy as was the burden placed on all branches of the armed forces, it is fair to say that the outbreak of the Korean war placed on the army works services one of the heaviest burdens of the subsequent expansion.
Let us now direct our attention to the accounting system used by the army works services and which Mr. Currie calls a good one. Late in 1947 the quartermaster general decided that a system of cost accounting should be introduced into the army works services. In response to his invitation, a senior officer of the quartermaster corps of the United States army came to Ottawa to give the benefit of his advice. Shortly afterwards an officer of the directorate of works and accommodation was sent to Montreal to discuss cost accounting systems with Anglin-Norcross Limited and the Foundation Company of Canada Limited. This officer was then sent to Washington to study in detail the system of cost accounting used by the United States army corps of engineers.
As a result of this study, it was decided that a modification of the system employed by the United States army corps of engineers would most nearly fit the needs of the army works services and work was put in hand to prepare the details of a system for introduction into the army works services. The new system was developed and introduced in the army works services in 1949.
At about the same time, the British and Australians also studied the United States army corps of engineers cost accounting system and we believe that they are introducing similar systems into their own army works services.
This cost accounting system had the following main objectives: (a) accounting for materials and supplies; (b) job costing; (c) real property records; (d) installed engineer fixture records; (e) work feature cost accounts.

Committee on Defence Expenditure
This system was approved in April, 1949. It was estimated that it would take at least a year and probably two years to put it into effect, provided, of course, that adequate staff would be available; so that if it had been possible to keep to the timetable the system would have been fully introduced by 1951. As it turned out, however, in June, 1950, Korea intervened and its challenging requirements had to be met.
The army works services was faced with the alternative of meeting that challenge with the resources available to them, or diverting their efforts in an attempt to achieve administrative perfection at the expense of operational performance. They really had no choice. They adopted the course which any soldier would choose and which I believe any Canadian would support. They met the operational requirements.
Both departmental audit reports and the Currie reports have indicated the presence of irregularities in the application of the accounting system. Difficulties have existed -and continue to exist-which have prevented the accounting system for the army works services from working satisfactorily. As is clear from the Currie report, the main difficulty has been to obtain qualified personnel to administer the system. This matter was referred to by the Solicitor General (Mr. Campney) in his speech on December 17.
The army works services experienced the same problems as those of private industry in obtaining graduate engineers and other qualified technical and accounting personnel. There was and is a shortage of engineers throughout the country; and with both industry and the armed forces expanding, the shortage has become acute and still is acute. In addition to this difficulty, the army was handicapped by the salaries which it could pay graduate engineers as compared to those offered by private industry. How significant is this shortage of qualified engineers may be appreciated when I tell you that in the army works services today there are 111 officers and that out of those 111, 53 are university graduates.
Consequently, the army works services was unable to obtain as rapidly as desired the service and civilian staff needed to do the job and also to keep the accounts in the way they should have been kept. In February, 1952, a special team of representatives of the civil service commission, the chief auditor's branch of the Department of National Defence and the Canadian army was set up to make a survey of the army works services establishments in order to arrive at the numbers and qualifications of the staff required to operate the system and to determine the rates of pay


which would have to be offered to attract the right type of person. Of course in the period following the institution of the system in 1949 there was not a moment when efforts were not being made both to create the right establishment and to recruit and enlist the staff required. This team to which I have referred completed surveys of the engineer detachments at Montreal, Ottawa, Kingston, Picton, Toronto and Camp Borden. As the Currie report indicates, and as our experience shows, this is a very necessary operation. It will be seen that in this particular respect the department and the army took action ten months before the report was delivered to me. However, Mr. Currie's investigation intervened, and as he was making a similar survey, and as there was urgent need for the service of the personnel involved to carry on with their own urgent regular tasks, this operation was suspended.
Since the Korean war began we have been short in the Department of National Defence at least 10 per cent of the civilians required at any time to fill the approved establishments-that is, within the whole department. That means that we have at all times been short between two thousand and four thousand civilian personnel.
A system of internal audit of the Department of National Defence was instituted in the month of February, 1948. It resulted from a study and report by representatives of treasury board, the comptroller of the treasury, the civil service commission and the department.
The position of chief auditor was advertised by the civil service commission and, in consequence of a competition which was held, Mr. J. A. Kidd was appointed. Mr. Kidd is a chartered accountant who had carried on his work in Saskatchewan before entering the service of the Auditor General. For some nineteen years he has been in the public service, mostly concerned with the Department of National Defence.
It should be emphasized that the chief auditor's branch carries on an internal audit of the work of the armed forces on behalf of the deputy minister. At the present time the chief auditor has a staff of 49 auditors and 19 others. Since the office was established the chief auditor has made a total of 1,185 reports. During the current fiscal year it is expected that about 350 audits will be made. Those audits are made of all units of the navy, army and air force, of the defence research board and of the inspection services.
The procedure is that the chief auditor prepares a report on each audit to the deputy minister. With respect to the army, a letter

is then sent to the chief of general staff in the name of the deputy minister, drawing attention to any matters which require action.
Prior to August 1950 these letters were addressed to the quartermaster general. Since then they have been addressed to the chief of general staff. Prior to January 1952 the practice had been to forward these reports through engineer channels, to the command engineer concerned, instructing him to take corrective action and report. Since January 1952 these reports have been forwarded by the chief of general staff to general officers commanding who have been reminded of their personal responsibility in this connection.
The general officer commanding is required to take corrective action and report. His report is reviewed by army headquarters and the staff of the deputy minister. Naturally it is not possible in an operation of this size for these reports or correspondence to be handled or even seen by the minister, or for that matter even by the deputy minister himself. It is only the really serious cases that the deputy minister can be expected to review personally.
On March 24, 1952, the chief auditor made a general report to the assistant deputy minister who has to do specially with financial matters. This was of course before Mr. Currie was asked to undertake an investigation, which was on April 21. In this memorandum to Mr. Armstrong, the assistant deputy minister in charge of financial matters, Mr. Kidd said in part:
The new system appears to have been well thought out and with proper supervision and staff should have been quite successful, but as indicated in a number of our audit reports, supervision has been almost entirely lacking and the quantity and quality of the staff inadequate. In five of the units visited it was claimed by officers in charge that insufficient and untrained staffs precluded carrying out the instructions properly while in seven other units tradesmen and labourers were observed performing accounting and stores duties. Some 95 officer positions on the establishment are said to be vacant.
Mr. Kidd then referred to corrective measures in progress:
Following the submission to the C.G.S. in February 1932 of an analysis of these general conditions, action was initiated which it is anticipated will eventually remedy the major faults.
(a)	The chief instructor of the R.C.E. school at Chilliwack, B.C., has been instructed to visit all commands to advise and assist works companies with respect to the accounting system.
(b)	At the request of the quartermaster general a survey team of three investigators from the civil service commission, assisted by representatives of the chief auditor, the D.C.P. (that is, the director of civilian personnel, an official of the Department of National Defence, Mr. Lavergne, reporting to the deputy minister) and the R.C.E. has been set up to
68108-60J
Committee on Defence Expenditure review the organization and staff requirements of the directorate of works and accommodation and works companies (Appendix B). It is understood that the civil service commission has been approached with a view to having the 95 vacant officer positions filled by civilian engineers, which in our opinion is a progressive move as the presence of one or more civilians in this capacity at each works company will make for continuity in the administrative staff and increased efficiency throughout the corps.
(c)	To meet the responsibility of internal audit and inspection required of the service, an establishment for a civilian inspection staff of seven has already been approved by the civil service commission.
(d)	It is understood that the D.W.A. (that is, the director of works and accommodation in the branch of the quartermaster general) on the instructions of the Q.M.G. is to prepare an analysis of our reports on which a general directive is to be prepared and sent to all works companies over the signature of the C.G.S.
It is therefore considered that everything possible has been or is being done to remedy the adverse conditions presently existing.
That is the end of the quotation, and the end of the memorandum. Mr. Currie himself said of Mr. Kidd that the chief auditor of the department had performed his functions conscientiously.
Attached to the report of Mr. Currie, as appendix B, is a table prepared by Mr. Kidd. Mr. Currie did not prepare it, and no changes were made in it after March 24,	1952,
although this table is the main evidence, apparently, of the breakdown given in Mr. Currie's report. You will recall that table. It has a column down the left, showing works companies and across the top are twenty different varieties of observations with X's underneath indicating the incidence of the observations.
Personally, I do not think "breakdown" as used in Mr. Currie's report is the right word. What we were trying to do was to work out an effective system of accounting. We simply did not have enough personnel to do that, and also to do the jobs which they were appointed to do. The system was only begun in 1949; but since the Korean war intervened in June of 1950, it was never possible for the army works services properly to implement the system, and at the same time to carry on the additional load imposed by the Korean war and sending the 27th brigade to Europe.
The breakdown to which Mr. Currie referred was, after all, a breakdown-if it was a breakdown-in keeping accounts, and not a breakdown in providing services and doing the essential work for which the army works services exists.
This table prepared by Mr. Kidd was attached by him to the memorandum dated March 24, 1952, to which I have just referred. Its purpose was to illustrate and emphasize the points he was making in his report,
940	HOUSE OF
Committee on Defence Expenditure ordinarily a confidential report, to the deputy minister, particularly the need tor additional supervisory staff. If you count the number of X's in this table, there being one X for each incident noted, you will see that altogether there are 154. They apply to most of the period during which the chief auditor was making audits of the units of the armed forces, including the army works service companies, and cover the work being done by 33 different detachments.
On my instructions the chief auditor and the judge advocate general have prepared a list summarizing the chief auditor's remarks in each one of these cases and then giving the explanation obtained from the unit and the resultant action taken. I have also had the judge advocate general look at these cases to see whether any further criminal prosecution should be laid or disciplinary action taken. He advises me that in his opinion there are only some 15 cases where there is evidence of the commission of a service offence. On my instructions the chief of the general staff is following up each one of these cases in the commands to see in what cases, if any, disciplinary action should be taken. So that you may see the character of the irregularities involved in these 15 cases let me read the note summarizing them, which is as follows:
Materials obtained or work started prior to authorization of project.
Requisitions on D.D.P. or L.P.O.'s split to keep within financial limits.
Accumulation of materials from completed works or materials removed from buildings not brought on charge in stock records.
Non-expendable stores issued to buildings without recording on installed fixture cards.
Unauthorized issue of stores and materials.
Failure to carry out stocktaking as required by the instructions.
Adjustment of discrepancies without reference to higher authority.
Estimated costs exceeded without review.
Cost of labour or materials charged against approved work orders not used on other jobs.
You will see that judged in the eyes of the civil courts and under criminal law these are not very serious crimes. But on the other hand they constitute things which should be stopped and which will be stopped in so far as it is possible.
However, right through, whether it be in the reports of the chief auditor, in the replies of the units or in the report of Mr. Currie, if I read them correctly and read his recommendations correctly, the main cause for all this has been a shortage of staff, particularly civilian staff, and in the services a shortage of engineering and accounting officers. Today in the army works services alone we are short approximately 1,700 civilian and 250 service personnel. That
[Mr. Claxton.l

is under the establishments as they were increased following the review to which I have referred.
Until we have this personnel on the strength it will not be possible to rectify the situation fully as you and I would like. Of course this shortage of staff has been known to the army, to the department and to the civil service commission. It has continually been a source of great concern. Both the department and the civil service commission have been making continuous efforts to obtain the staff that was needed to do the job. An effort was made to get technical staff from other government departments, but without marked success. In addition to the usual advertisements of vacancies the civil service has repeatedly made special efforts to obtain applicants. As recently as September 4, 1952, the commission advised the department as follows:
It is felt that your technical directorates must be prepared to carry on with a shortage of staff in these fields since industrial agencies at the moment are required to do so.
The device mentioned by the Auditor General in his report of borrowing qualified personnel from civilian firms under special contract is possible on a limited scale in order to get special jobs done, but cannot work satisfactorily in accomplishing routine continuing operations in the works service, even if the personnel could be obtained.
The fact is that the expansion of the armed forces, the partial introduction of a new accounting system, the shortage of qualified personnel to administer it, the activities of 24 civilian contractors engaged on 37 major contracts at Petawawa during 1950-51 and 1951-52 combined to create a situation at Petawawa of which, as Mr. Currie says, a handful of crooks took advantage.
May I turn now to the recommendations made by Mr. Currie in his report.
Before the minister does that, will he permit a question?
I am following a consecutive order. I will answer the hon. member's question later.
This question has to do with responsibility. Has the minister any information in answer to the $48 question as to who changed the words "at or near the top," which were so singularly altered?

That does not arise out of anything that I have said. If there was any change of that character made it was made by Mr. Currie on his own responsibility before he signed the report. If my hon. friend has confidence in Mr. Currie, then he cannot have

it both ways. If Mr. Currie decided to make the change it was because he decided that that change was desirable to be made.
May I turn now to the recommendations which are to be found at pages 728 to 730 of Hansard. They are 44 in number and were referred to by the Solicitor General in his speech. But perhaps I should bring the information on them up to date.
As I have said already, I believe that Mr. Currie, his associates and those in the department and the army regarded this whole operation as a co-operative effort to arrive at the causes and prevent their recurrence. The extent to which this project has been carried out by the department is indicated by the action which was taken before the delivery of the report. The extent to which the recommendations had already been put into effect was referred to by the Solicitor General.
Of the 44 recommendations made, 27 were being put into effect before the report was made or received by the department. Four more recommendations are regarded as urgent and will be carried out as additional manpower becomes available. Eight recommendations involve additional manpower and also involve very considerable sums of money, possibly more than any potential advantage would justify. These will be subject to further consideration. Three recommendations do not involve additional manpower and money but will require further study. One of the recommendations is not considered desirable to implement except in respect of new major developments, and one other appears to be unsuitable as it is phrased.
Having given a summary, it seems to me that hon. members might wish me to give, under the five main divisions already mentioned, Mr. Currie's recommendations and the comments of the department in each case. It would be very convenient if these could be printed in Hansard in parallel columns, but I am aware that that is really not in accordance with the practice of the house and I am not going to ask for unanimous consent that it be done. But I do inform the house that the comments on these recommendations which have been made in detail by the officials of the department are available and will be put before the committee on defence expenditure when it meets.
I do not need to tell hon. members that most of the recommendations will entail considerable increases in manpower and expenditure. With regard to the appendix in the Currie report proposing an increased staff at Petawawa, the new establishment for Petawawa, with the exception of the estimator recommended by Mr. Currie, was designed in November, 1951, by the department in cooperation with other government agencies,
Committee on Defence Expenditure and the only addition of consequence made by Mr. Currie is that of the office of estimator. The establishment at Petawawa was increased from 23 military and 142 civilians to 35 military and 223 civilians. The increase in the army works services establishment at Petawawa was necessary because of the expansion of the army which led to the creation of home stations for two regiments and ancillary units at the station.
The increases in the army works services establishment at Petawawa and elsewhere were not in consequence of the Currie report but were initiated prior to the report to bring the army works services up to the strength required to do its job. Altogether these increases and those recommended in the report, because Mr. Currie incorporates these increases in his own recommendations, resulted in an increase from 1,088 military and 3,436 civilians to 1,109 military and 5,123 civilians, an increase of 21 military and 1,687 civilians. But at the present time, as I have indicated, on other establishments within the army works services in round figures we are short a total of 1,700 civilians and some 250 service personnel.
The increases involve an annual expenditure of approximately $5,246,000. The major portion of this increased engineer work load was due to the large number of civilians required for the operation of utility plants. The need to provide central warehousing was provided for in the approved 1952-53 annual estimates and new accommodation for companies and detachments was provided for in the approved 1951-52 estimates.
The report makes a number of recommendations regarding additional security measures. Many of these have already been put into effect and, of course, they will all be given consideration. I would be surprised, however, if we do not find that in some cases the cost of the full measure indicated would be out of all proportion to any reduction in losses which might result, and this of course is an important practical consideration. The theft at Farnham is a striking example of what I mean. The cost of providing good security over the period of six years after the camp ceased to be used would have been about forty times the loss suffered by the public through the theft of the property for which prosecutions were laid. It is always necessary to strike a balance between the cost of security and the possibility of loss.
Leaving aside such recommendations in the report as involve the complete relocation of gates, campsites, roads, compounds, et cetera, most of which are out of the question, and taking into consideration only those directly
942	HOUSE OF
Committee on Defence Expenditure related to storage and safekeeping of engineering supplies and equipment, we have estimated that the additional cost merely for security fences at Petawawa alone would be $286,000 with an annual recurring cost for additional guards of $119,000. We have also completed estimates for another typical company at a similar establishment, namely, Camp Borden, where we estimate that the capital cost for fences would be $346,000, with an additional annual recurring cost of $139,000.
Applying these figures on a proportionate basis to other army works establishments, we arrive at an estimate of the capital cost for additional security and safekeeping facilities for army works services installations alone of $1,774,000, with an additional annual recurring cost for guards alone of $1,106,000. It may be pointed out also that, as we have said, in none of the cases at Petawawa was the loss attributable to lack of physical security. The degree of security must of necessity be related to the nature of the stores. Here the materials stolen were scrap, build-ding materials, salvaged articles, et cetera. To what extent that additional manpower and expenses would be justified by the results may be open to question. Certainly, as I say, we must see to it that every justifiable measure that can be taken is taken to safeguard the people's property.
In addition to the steps to which I have referred which are in line with Mr. Currie's recommendations, I might mention a number of other things which we have done in connection with the army works services.
(a)	A revised establishment has been created in the quartermaster general's branch regarding works and quartering.
(b)	New establishments have been created for each works company and new stores depots.
(c)	The army works services detachment at Petawawa has been raised to the status of a company, which has the effect of putting it under command headquarters and eliminating the channel through the area headquarters at Kingston.
(d)	The civil service commission has approved the establishment for civilian personnel officers in the field directly responsible to the director of civilian personnel in the Department of National Defence.
(e)	A board has been set up consisting of three senior army officers, a representative of the civil service commission and of the director of civilian personnel, which will visit army units with a view to examining their establishments and arriving at much more speedy decisions.


(f)	The quartermaster general's branch has established a travelling inspection division which will follow up reports made by the chief auditor to see on the spot that desirable recommendations are immediately implemented without waiting for correspondence.
I come now to the series of 33 regulations which Mr. Currie says were broken. Reference is made to these at page 715 of the report as it appears in Hansard. Mr. Currie does not say when these breaches of regulations occurred but one can assume from the context that he relates them to the irregularities at Petawawa, though some of them may also have occurred elsewhere. I have asked the judge advocate general and the Department of Justice if there is anything in the report of Mr. Currie or anything brought out at the trials or in the police reports which would justify instituting additional prosecutions of service or civilian personnel, or taking any additional kind of disciplinary action in this connection. I have an opinion as regards criminal prosecutions from the deputy minister of justice and as regards disciplinary action and criminal prosecutions from the judge advocate general that, apart from the cases I have mentioned and some others that are the subject of further investigation, the only thing that might be indicated would be further disciplinary actions.
In concluding my reference to the Currie report, I should like to draw your attention to the paragraph with which he begins part IV, "Conclusions and Recommendations". He says:
My report, I fully recognize, contains many discouraging features. The over-all situation is. however, by no means discouraging because of the fact that the cure for what has gone wrong in the past can be and, in fact, is being applied.
In my remarks I have endeavoured to give you the background so that you can understand the circumstances through which the grave irregularities which occurred at Petawawa did in fact take place. In giving this explanation do not think for a second that I wish to excuse or condone either the fact that the irregularities did take place or the fact that they could have taken place.
There are in this house a great many veterans of the two wars. They know, and the veterans all over this country-and there are a lot of them-know, and I think the public has a pretty good idea too that an army is not a Sunday school and soldiers are not saints. That does not mean that we should condone wrongdoing, but neither does it mean that you can expect to have an army in which all the officers and men behave perfectly. There are bound to be occasional

misdemeanours and unfortunately there is also bound to be a certain amount of wrongdoing just as there is in the rest of the population.
Canadians have won for their arms a fine record in the first and second world wars- and now in Korea. What they have done has been accomplished because of their qualities, and that includes the quality of their leadership. Field leaders are selected because of their qualities of decision, of command, yes, of courage and initiative, and not primarily because of their superior ability as storekeepers or accountants. Yet each one of these has to have, in addition to his responsibilities for training and leading the formations under his command, responsibilities for the administration of what in civilian life would be a very large business operation.
Mr. Currie in his report has said that the amounts involved at Petawawa were probably not large. The estimate given to me by the police was that the total involved was probably less than $50,000. That is still their view. A very large part of all that was stolen has been recovered and the guilty have been prosecuted and punished.
What remains to be done is to ensure that any steps which are likely to bring results sufficiently important to justify the men and money involved should be taken and taken without delay and as fast as qualified personnel can be obtained. That will not ensure a complete cessation of irregularities and pilfering and even fraud and theft in operations of this magnitude. Unfortunately, we all know that these things do go on in civilian as well as military activities.
I would like to add, however, that the records put before the defence expenditure committee at its last session, and the information made available to me, indicate that the scale of losses due to service activities having regard to the value of the property involved are not any larger than those commonly experienced in civilian activities of a similar character.
Despite the fact that our operations are many times larger, I think you would find that the loss by thefts and pilferage in the armed forces is no larger than that in the major commercial undertakings of the country. When any one of these suffers a loss very little is said about it in the press or parliament, but it is seldom indeed that a loss occurs or a member of the armed forces commits a crime that it is not blazoned in print across the country.
Now, in consequence of this report and of the action we have taken and of the actions we will take, I hope that we can both improve the organization and increase the personnel
Committee on Defence Expenditure so as to reduce our losses to the lowest possible figure. That is our constant aim and goal.
However, irrespective of the action we shall take, we shall continue to have losses, losses which, because of the size and nature of the operation, will appear to be very considerable indeed, but which, when viewed fairly and with a sense of proportion, will not be unreasonable. And if I may say so, we shall continue to have those losses no matter who is minister of national defence, even if the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) were minister of national defence, or the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).
It won't be long now.

I believe that the view I have just expressed will be confirmed by an experienced accountant like the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart).
We shall also continue to try to find ways and means of improving the organization of the armed forces and of the Department of National Defence. Now that the great majority of contracts for construction and orders for equipment have been placed and that we have so large a proportion of the manpower required throughout the armed forces as a whole, we will have more time, I hope, to spend on examining and improving and streamlining still further.
In view of the importance attached to this report and for the reasons already mentioned by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), I move, seconded by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson):
That the motion be amended by inserting after the words "March 31, 1950", in the fourth line thereof, the following:
"and initially to give priority in their examination to the expenditures and commitments of the Canadian army works services as dealt with in the report of G. S. Currie, Esquire, chartered accountant, tabled in the House of Commons on December 15, 1952."

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I raise a point of order? May I make it clear that my point of order relates only to procedure and not to the substance of the proposed amendment. I will deal with that later.
My point of order is as to whether or not the amendment of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) is in order. I draw Your Honour's attention to a citation in Beauchesne's third edition which you have often read against us on this side of the house when we have sought to move an amendment to motions setting up committees. Citation 546 reads:
When the house is engaged in nominating the members of a committee, it is not competent for an hon. member to open the whole subject.

Committee on Defence Expenditure
I read that paragraph in order to put the whole citation on the record although it is the next paragraph which counts:
When the house is considering a motion, of which notice has been given, for the appointment of a select committee, a member cannot move in amendment that the committee be given wider powers than those which were set down in the notice. On the 13th March 1938,-
I interject to say that there is an error at that point; it should read 1939-
__a minister moved that a special committee be
appointed to study the question of redistribution of electoral districts and to enquire into the methods whereby the source of campaign funds may be traceable. Two amendments were moved: one proposed that the committee's powers be extended so as to investigate amounts of contributions over $100 for the past ten years; the , other proposed to investigate the methods whereby lumbermen, fishermen, seamen and miners in British Columbia may be enabled to exercise their franchise.
The Speaker ruled both amendments out of order on the ground that they raised new questions not contemplated in the notice of motion and proposed to extend the committee's powers far beyond those set down in the notice, and also that the necessity of giving notice will be nullified if such notice is not used as a guidance for the decision of the house.
If I had thought, Mr. Speaker, that any attempt would be made at this point to move an amendment of this character I would, of course, have had a number of references ready to quote by page number, and by chapter and verse. I did not do that. But in my own mind I can recall that when the motion was made to set up a committee to go into the question of old age security an attempt was made from this side of the house to move amendments to that motion, and Your Honour ruled those amendments out of order on the basis of the citation that I have just read. Similarly, a year or so ago, when there was a motion to set up a special committee on veterans affairs, the terms of reference of which were more restrictive than they had been on previous occasions, an attempt was made by the member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) and by my deskmate the member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) to move amendments. Those amendments were ruled out of order, again on the basis of citation 546.
I recall also that in the session of 1952 the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) had on the order paper a motion for the setting up of a special committee on redistribution. I recall that after he had given notice of that motion there were certain changes he wanted to make in it. If my memory serves me correctly, he stated in the house that the reason he withdrew his motion and submitted another one through the usual channels of giving notice was that he was aware of this very citation and of the difficulty, if not the


impropriety, of amending a motion to set up a committee once it has been placed on the order paper and had been moved in the house. As I say, Mr. Speaker, it was because of the action the Prime Minister took with respect to the motion for a redistribution committee last year that I could not imagine that any member on the government side would try this today. I did not, therefore, assemble these references page by page, but I am sure that Your Honour recalls them and they can be found if necessary.
I believe it is obvious, whether or not we agree with the substance of the amendment, that what happens when an' amendment is moved in this way is that the question is placed before us without the required forty-eight hours' notice being given. At the same time, I may say that I do not see that the amendment is at all necessary, which is another procedural argument. After all, you are not supposed to move amendments that are unnecessary. I submit there are already sufficient powers contained in the motion as it is worded to enable the committee to send for papers and records, one of them being the Currie report. They can also send for persons, including Mr. Currie himself. So, Mr. Speaker, on the grounds of citation 546, and the ground that no notice has been given of this, I think it is out of order. There is also the ground that it is unnecessary because the power to send for persons, papers and records is already contained in the Prime Minister's motion.

There is another consideration that I would submit should be borne in mind, Mr. Speaker, in giving consideration to this amendment. We have had on the order paper now for some considerable time a notice of motion in the name of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). The Prime Minister did not choose to speak when the motion was called and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) spoke on behalf of the government. Every hon. member in this house has had reason to assume that the motion we would be considering this afternoon as presented by the government would be the motion on the order paper. The effect of this is to place before the house a new motion by the government without notice.
I would point out also to Your Honour the fact that on a procedure of this kind the notice stands in the name of the Prime Minister, but the Minister of National Defence addressed his remarks to that motion and then moved an amendment which every hon. member knows will be supported by the members of the party who have shown a

strong disinclination to show any independence of opinion in their voting in this house.

If this amendment is allowed to stand what can happen is that a motion to set up a committee with certain terms of reference may be brought down in the house by a minister. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that you might find some assistance there in determining this question, because it is obvious from what I have read that the practice as outlined by Sir Erskine May is to give instructions to a committee after the committee has been set up, and not during the course of the setting up of the committee.

I hesitate to add my small voice to those of the experts who have already spoken, but it occurs to me that one quotation which I think is pertinent has not yet been submitted to Your Honour. We have before us and are discussing a notice of motion. Citation 315 of Beauchesne, third edition, reads as follows:
A modification of a notice of motion standing upon the notice paper is permitted, if the amended notice does not exceed the scope of the original notice. A new notice must be given in the Votes and Proceedings under standing order 45, when a material change is to be made to a notice of motion before it is taken up by the house.
The question here seems to be whether or not a material change is to be made. As one


who sat through the sessions of a very similar committee constituted under a very similar original notice of motion at the last session of this house, it was most noticeable that a great deal of the time of the committee, set up to examine all expenditures of public moneys for national defence, was taken in examining the details and the circumstances of pilferings, irregularities, losses, fires, etc., matters such as I think we all agree are the main subject of the Currie report.
Therefore to refer the Currie report to this committee is surely not exceeding the scope of the original notice of motion in the name of the Prime Minister, at least not exceeding it as it was interpreted by the committee during the last session. If that is the case, then surely it is in order unless it is so valueless as to be useless, and I would suggest that the word "might" in citation 407 does not involve a question of compulsion but refers to the opportunity of the committee to do or not to do something.
The other point that has been raised in this connection, and which worries me because I do not know very much about it, is the suggestion that if a notice of motion of this sort stands on the order paper apparently no one on this side should move an amendment because presumably-if this is not the argument I do not know what it is-by doing so the chance is lost to the opposition of moving an amendment. If I understand this discussion correctly, that surely does not make sense because it certainly seems to me that all that has to be done is to dispose of the first amendment in order to move another or at the moment, provided it is legally competent for some member to do so, to move a subamendment, dispose of the subamendment and the amendment, and move another one.
Surely no one is trying to suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that once a notice appears on the order paper the sole right to move any amendment to it must rest with those who, because of circumstances, represent the minority in the house. Mr. Speaker, may I point out that what the hon. member has said he quite correctly has stated makes no sense. I have sought to point out that our procedure recognizes the division of the house into the government side and the opposition side. I sought to point out that the government in presenting a motion puts forward a proposition. It is then customary for the opposition to have an opportunity to deal with that primary motion and to attach to that motion such modifying amendment as in their opinion will improve the subject matter before the house.

I have only sought to indicate to you the effect of a decision in accordance with the argument that has been made, but under no circumstances would I wish to leave the impression that I was in any way limiting the independence of members on the other side of the house, which I would wish to see increased greatly day by day.

Committee on Defence Expenditure in declaring it out of order. That is not a matter which I must determine at this time.
Another point was raised-in fact I suggested it-with respect to the value of the amendment and whether it added anything to the motion or directed the committee in its procedures; but from the citation in May you will notice that the house has power to direct a committee as to its procedure. The point therefore that remains to be determined is the reference made to citation 407 in Beauchesne, third edition, which reads as follows:

I would state again that if in my opinion this amendment empowered the committee to do something which it otherwise could not do I would rule it out of order. However, the committee might not see fit to consider those things. This motion would direct the committee to consider the expenditures and commitments mentioned in the Currie report.
In my opinion this house has the power to direct the committee to do so, and for the reasons I have stated I must rule that the amendment is in order.
