That reform or improvement is that so far in this session every time a divorce bill has been called for second reading, at least it has been the case that the evidence has been printed and placed in our hands. That was one minor point that we used to complain about, namely that we were asked to proceed with these bills before we had the evidence. I hope the fact that that has been overcome means that attention is being given to the whole problem and that it will not be long before these and other divorce bills are dealt with in a more proper way.
Shall the motion carry?
On division.
Motion agreed to, bills read the second time and referred to the standing committee on miscellaneous private bills.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48    VOLUNTARY REVOCABLE CHECK- OFF OF UNION DUES

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre) moved
speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48    VOLUNTARY REVOCABLE CHECK- OFF OF UNION DUES
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 2, to amend the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act (voluntary revocable check-off).

He said: Mr. Speaker, if I had hope that this bill would pass as readily as did the first private bill which came up today, or as readily as the thirty divorce bills just dealt with, I would refrain from saying anything at this time. I do hope that one of these times this bill will be given its second reading and referred to the standing committee on industrial relations so that progress may be made in writing into our national labour code a provision for the voluntary revocable check-off.
As I have indicated on previous occasions when this bill has been before the house, it is a measure which asks for a legislative enactment to provide the very minimum of what is known as union security. There are a number of ways in which union security can be provided, and I want to say that for my part I would like to see something even more effective and more useful than what is asked for in this bill. But at least this is a minimum form of union security, and it is already in effect in the labour codes of a number of provinces in this country. I have reminded the house on previous occasions of the fact that all parties in this house have, on various occasions, expressed their support of the principle of union security. In fact, all the opposition parties have been voting for this bill for several years now, and indeed there have been a fair number of members on the Liberal side of the house who, when a vote has been called, have stood up and voted for it. I am only surprised that the number of Liberals has been so few-it got as high as 17 two years ago-for at the last national Liberal convention, the one held here in Ottawa in 1948, it was made part of that party's platform that it stood for union security.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the provision in the bill is quite simple. It specifies that where a union is certified under the provisions of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, that union may request the checkoff. If it does it means that the company is required to deduct from the pay of employees their trade union dues, and pay them over to the union, but, only in the cases of those individual employees who indicate in writing that it is their desire that it be done. In addition to that provision, it is stipulated that after any person has directed that his dues be checked off in that way he can, at a later date, revoke that decision if he wishes to do so. In other words, that is the reason for the way in which this provision is defined, namely as the voluntary revocable check-off.
As I have already said, this is only a minimum way in which to guarantee union
Industrial Relations
security, but at least it is a beginning. I have pointed out on previous occasions that this matter has been requested year by year by the major labour congresses in their representations to the government. I have no doubt but that it will be included in the representations they will make to the government again this year. I point out also that this is a provision in many of the provincial labour codes.
The only active opposition to this provision, so far as the federal law is concerned, of which we have been aware in recent years has been the occasional mimeographed circular distributed to the members of this house by the Railway Association of Canada. This association is, of course, an association of the employers, and that association from time to time has objected to this bill. The objection has been largely on the ground that it would involve considerable bookkeeping. It has been pointed out in this house, not only by myself but by the member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) and others who have supported this measure, that that is really a rather specious argument, particularly in view of the fact that employers make a great many other deductions at the request of their employees.
Well, to me it is significant that no such protest against this bill has been received as yet this year from the Railway Association of Canada. I dare to think that the reason no such protest has come is because of the ruling of the board that dealt recently with the railway dispute between the railway companies and their non-operating employees. Hon. members will recall that that board was headed by Mr. Justice R. L. Kellock, and the other two members were Mr. Paul S. Smith, appointed by the employers, and Mr. David Lewis, appointed by the employees. Majority and minority reports were presented. In other words, there were many points on which there was disagreement between Mr. Justice Kellock and Mr. Smith, on the one hand, and Mr. Lewis on the other. However, at least this question of the checkoff was one upon which they were agreed. Mr. Lewis, in his minority report, pointed out that he would like to see an even greater measure of union security for railway employees than just the check-off, but at least he was glad to join with Mr. Justice Kellock and Mr. Smith in recommending that the check-off, so far as railway employees are concerned, be instituted.
Reference to this provision in the majority report is found on page 43. The significant sentence reads as follows:
With regard to the check-off, the board is of opinion that, as every employee now has the same

Industrial Relations
right as any other creditor to assign the whole or any part of any debt, present or future owing to him, the proposed clause is one that should properly form part of the new agreements.
I understand that on the basis of that report the check-off will shortly be in effect so far as railway employees are concerned. There is some question as to whether it will be on the basis of the Rand formula. At least what we are asking for in this bill is being accepted now by the railway companies of Canada, and in this case by their non-operating employees.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that since this group of employees constitutes perhaps the largest number of employees who come under federal labour jurisdiction, there is now no reason at all why there should be any reluctance or any resistance on the part of the government to writing this measure into the federal labour code. The wording of the section that would be added by the terms of my bill is, in fact, the wording that was drawn in the Department of Labour. The story behind that, briefly, is that in 1948 when the industrial relations committee was dealing with the federal code it was moved by the hon. member for Spadina, as a member of that committee, that the check-off provision be written into the labour code at that time. His motion carried, although it was on a very close division. After his motion carried, although it did not have the support of Mr. Mitchell, then minister of labour, the minister had one of his officials come back the next day and suggest that if this provision were to be written into the code perhaps it would be well to have it written in language that the legal advisers of the Department of Labour thought most appropriate.
The hon. member for Spadina accepted the language drafted by the legal officers of the Department of Labour, and it is that language which forms the main part of the bill now before us. Some members may wonder what happened to that provision which was written into the labour code in 1948. The fact is that when the bill came back to the house to be considered in committee of the whole, a private member on the government side moved that that clause which had been written into the bill in the committee be deleted. After considerable debate in this house that amendment carried and the provision which we thought we had won was stricken from the national labour code.
As I have already said, support for this measure has been growing. The number of members who voted to keep that clause in the bill in 1948 was 35. The next time there was a vote on this proposal was in 1950, when 45 members voted for it. The next vote came in 1951, on February 28, when
IMr. Knowles.]
67 members voted for it, and included in those 67 were all the members of the opposition groups who were present and 17 members on the government side of the house plus the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson).
I am encouraged by that growth in support for this measure from year to year. I am encouraged also by the fact that this principle has now been accepted by the railway companies and by the employees. I hope that on this occasion we will not have the kind of argument against it that we have had on previous occasions, but that the house will agree to the second reading of this bill so that it may go to the standing committee on industrial relations for consideration by that committee.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48    VOLUNTARY REVOCABLE CHECK- OFF OF UNION DUES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks of the sponsor of this bill on the revocable check-off. Two years ago a similar bill was introduced by the same hon. member. At that time I had occasion to make a few comments in this house with regard to the provision not only of the check-off or the nature of the checkoff that was introduced in the bill at that time, but also with regard to my interpretation of the thinking of trade union people as to the type and the character of the check-off they required to give them the kind of union security they would need in order to have a healthy trade union organization.
I do not wish to be insular in again speaking on a trade union subject in this chamber, but I believe at this time we should review some of the matters that have been discussed on this question. I should like to take this opportunity to say that I was greatly impressed by the remarks made in the previous debate by our present Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg). On this occasion I desire to place on the record what I believe to be pertinent information with regard to the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, and I am going to take a couple of minutes to read into the record from page 639 of Hansard for February 23, 1951, an extract which I believe indicates responsible thinking with regard to the check-off. At that time the Minister of Labour had this to say:
If today parliament steps in to legislate on such matters as the check-off, another parliament at another time may attempt to settle the issue in quite a different way. Present legislation adequately promotes free collective bargaining and parliament should consider carefully before going beyond this point by resolving issues which parties to collective bargaining can best resolve themselves.
The ideal behind any industrial relations legislation, I believe, in a free enterprise economy is the promotion of sound industrial self-government. We

may not possibly come nearer to that goal by legislating on such substantive terms of employment as the check-off.
Then the minister went on to say:
The more I study it, and the more I see the operation of our Canadian Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, the more I like it and the more I feel that we should go slow in unnecessarily making it a policeman for either bargaining party. It may not be a perfect act, but there are not many things in the world that are perfect-
I agree with those words of the Minister of Labour. I would say that the act may not be perfect, but I would also say that in its present form it is the best means yet devised to produce a good climate for labour and management to meet in and to decide their differences responsibly.
In 1951 I said that I believed in the checkoff that was negotiated, not one that was legislated. No one knows better than do trade unionists and management that there must be good will in every document that is executed and signed by both parties. At that time, of one union for which I had a great deal of respect, I said that when they again opened their contract for negotiations with management, they would be able to negotiate the kind of check-off that would be acceptable to the people embraced by that agreement, both at the management level and at the employee level. I do not like to take this occasion in the House of Commons to say that at that time I was right, as has been proven by the fact that just recently 17 major railway organizations were able to meet management around the bargaining table like gentlemen, to discuss their problems, to find ways and means of settling their differences, to include a checkoff which goes far beyond the kind of innocuous check-off that is suggested in the bill before us, then to sign an agreement for a stipulated period of time and to work under that agreement with good will.
Now that it has been proven to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) that matters of this kind can be negotiated, I am surprised that he should still pursue this question and persist in endeavouring to persuade the members in this chamber to support an innocuous kind of check-off that is not nearly as good as that which trade unionists and management have been able to agree on in recent months. In other words, if this provision is written into the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, it would not only be a floor but a ceiling, and it certainly is not as good as what the unionists themselves and management have been able to agree on.
I am grateful to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre for affording me the
Industrial Relations
opportunity of saying, two years subsequent to 1951, that what I said in the chamber at that time has borne fruit and that my thinking on this question has been proven to be correct. Because I have the confidence of many trade unions people and am able to interpret their thinking correctly, I was able to suggest that subsequent to 1951 an agreement, which the men and management would say embodied good will, would be signed by both parties and would include a proper form of check-off.
I believe I said in 1951 that discussions of this type are useful. This one certainly serves a useful purpose in allowing me to tell Mr. Speaker and hon. members, and particularly the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, that the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act has worked very well since 1948. I am confident that it will work well in the future, and that it allows the widest possible scope for labour and management to meet in a healthy atmosphere, and to arrive at agreements with good will. It will allow those in industry, including those engaged in transportation services, opportunities to work under collective agreements, and to enjoy the very best of working conditions made possible by legislation placed on the statute books by a federal administration.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48    VOLUNTARY REVOCABLE CHECK- OFF OF UNION DUES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the second time I have taken the opportunity to speak on a measure of this kind. I recall that when a similar measure was discussed last year I said that to a certain extent it would diminish if not extinguish the sovereignty of unions. I saw a smile on the face of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), and even on the face of the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll). I have not forgotten those smiles.
During the recess I took the trouble to find out if I was the only one who thought as I think in this matter. To my support I bring the good opinion of a very strong socialist in France, Daniel Guerin, who has written a book in two volumes entitled Ou va le Peuple Americain?-"Where are the American people going?" In this book I found valuable information. If I am not too far out of order I would say that from the book I learned that the first sit-down strike occurred in 1914, and that a second one developed in 1923 by Mussolini in Milan and Turin. However, I must not go too far in making reference to the information I got from the book, because in doing so I would be out of order.

Industrial Relations
I should like, however, to place on record Mr. Guerin's opinion of the check-off. At page 217 of the first volume he says:
The employers deduct from the payroll of the workers belonging to a syndicate the amount of syndical contributions, and send it to the syndicate. This combination is eminently favourable to syndical bureaucracy-
And this from a socialist!
-because it insures the latter, in a comfortable chair, the regular coming in of funds. But the check-off has the worse inconvenience of deepening the ditch between the base and the direction of the syndicalized world.
Again I say that this is a socialist speaking.
It establishes the employer, as Daniel de Leon said, as some kind of treasurer of the United States.
And Daniel de Leon was another socialist in the United States.
The worker is under the impression that the fists, the patronate and the syndicate are but one and the same immense, anonymous machine, firmly installed above him, and against which he can do nothing. In not paying his contributions directly to the syndicate, or to his agent, on the very place of labour, he loses the habit, if he had it, of going to the office of the organization. He does not look at it as if it was his, and his connection with the syndicate's agent in the manufacture stays weak.
That is the opinion of a good socialist who has spent two and a half years making a survey in the United States. He looked into the capitalist world in that country, the formation of workers' unions, the situation of the coloured people, and the agricultural situation in the southern part of the United States. This is his opinion, an opinion absolutely unfavourable to the check-off. As my hon. friend has just said, I am not against the voluntary check-off, the check-off that develops after a getting together of employees and employers, after friendly discussion and friendly agreement within the union, when employers are prepared to accept the check-off and to bring it within the bounds of a special industry.
I think favourably of that procedure, and for this reason, that when there is an understanding between employers and employees there is at the same time a development of that friendship that is so greatly needed between these two groups in the community. We need that friendship and that perfect understanding because in the world, in Canada, there are those who live on misunderstandings between employers and employees. There is a philosophy that thrives on social unrest and misery. It thrives, too, on misunderstandings between employers and employees. It is certainly worth-while if employers and employees can get together more often and come to an understanding on points affecting an industry or a syndicate. It is beneficial to all concerned if a

spirit of friendship can be developed between them, so that the syndical and the employers' worlds may understand each other better.
That is what we need, and that is why I ask at this time that the check-off be not given approval through a law passed by parliament, but rather that it be permitted to operate in certain industries on a basis of free and friendly understanding. This is the second time I have given my opinion in this connection. I was more interested, however, in placing before the house the opinion of a socialist who shares the philosophy of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, and to point out that even the advocates of that philosophy entertain differences of opinion as to the desirability of imposing by force of law the provision for check-off in this country. I hope the measure will not pass this year.

speakeroldname: Mr. Paul E. Cote (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48    VOLUNTARY REVOCABLE CHECK- OFF OF UNION DUES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on several occasions I have voiced my views on the principle of this bill. In fact this is the fourth time that a bill to amend the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act has been presented for this purpose. I should like to make a few remarks tonight which I did not have the opportunity to develop at any length in the past.
At the outset I wish to assure my hon. friend that I have nothing against the checkoff of union dues, in itself, or against any stronger measures of union security. On the contrary, I fully approve the principle of those measures. If there is anything within my control that I can do to increase the number of contracts in industry containing provisions for union security or the check-off of union dues I shall never hesitate to do it.
May I say to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) that I think the criterion which should guide this chamber in deciding whether this bill is desirable should be this. Is the underlying principle of this bill consistent with the basic principles of the act it intends to amend? From the arguments which have been advanced in support of the passing of this bill I am inclined to believe that this important aspect of the question has not been examined as it ought to have been and that no convincing case has been made to justify the change which it advocates in the statute at this time.
The Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act embodies basic principles which should not be altered without reasonable cause or without applying the same measure of caution which was applied in the

drafting and passing of that act. Those principles are freedom of association, certification of bargaining units, free collective bargaining on all matters subject to agreement between employers and employees, and compulsory compliance by both parties with the machinery set up for the settlement of all disputes.
Union security provisions, including any measure of check-off of union dues, have hitherto been considered as matters for collective bargaining. It is true as some hon. members have said, more particularly in this debate the sponsor of the bill, that in six provinces the labour relations acts include provisions for the voluntary revocable checkoff. But in discussing the bill no one has given any indication as to what procedure was followed, whether management was consulted and had agreed or what was the situation as far as the check-off was concerned, in the provinces where such provisions were included in the labour acts.
Four important provinces, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Ontario and Quebec-the last two being the most highly industrialized provinces-have not yet deemed it to be in the best interests of good labour-management relations to enact such a provision. In the attitude which these provinces have taken, to stand by the principle of free collective bargaining, they are in complete accord with the federal act. They still believe that the time has not yet come to introduce any compulsory feature in the field of collective bargaining, that if they did this without previous consultation and a certain measure of agreement with and by both parties in industry they would be setting a precedent of unilateral if not arbitrary statutory action which might become dangerous in the future, in that it could be invoked by some other government for legislative action which might not be in the best interests of trade unions and of labour-management relations in this country. Once a legislative body has determined by statute and made compulsory a provision which is normally dealt with by collective bargaining it opens the door for more and more intrusions of the same kind by the state in a field which ought to belong exclusively to labour-management negotiations.
I have in mind to say a few words this afternoon on the recently-concluded agreement between the railroad companies and the employee brotherhoods, but I shall leave this until the concluding part of my speech.
I should like to remind my hon. friends that trade unions have gained in importance, in strength and in influence during the past decade to an amazing degree. If one reads the Labour Gazette today he will have an
Industrial Relations
opportunity of realizing each month what this increased strength of the trade unions has brought by way of benefits to their membership. This is a clear indication that through the bargaining process the unions have succeeded in getting what was in the interests of their rank and file.
The principle of free collective bargaining is the cornerstone of the federal labour relations act. That should not be altered, any more than any other major provision in the act, without consultation with and at least a certain measure of agreement by both parties who will be affected by the change. That was the purpose of the then minister of labour, the late Hon. Humphrey Mitchell, when he submitted the initial draft of his legislation to the national bodies of management and labour.
On the one hand there was the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, the Canadian Congress of Labour, the dominion legislative council of railway transportation brotherhoods and the Canadian Confederation of Catholic Syndicates, representing labour. On the other hand there was the Canadian Manufacturers Association, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, the Railway Association of Canada and the Canadian Construction Association, on the management side. The measure of agreement on the major provisions of the act which was then obtained from both sides was indeed gratifying. This consensus of opinion gave the assurance that the legislation was initiated on solid ground and should not be altered in its major provisions without determining and following the best possible procedure which would tend to safeguard the prerogatives of all concerned.
The initial draft of the labour act was submitted to and approved in its broad principles by the provincial ministers of labour. There was no necessity to do this, but the late Humphrey Mitchell showed wisdom in availing himself of the opportunity provided by a conference which was taking place with his colleagues in the provinces on other matters to seek their views and secure their agreement on the main features of the bill which was then being considered. This consultation has paved the way for the inclusion of section 62, which tends to promote as much uniformity of legislation as possible between the two levels of government and to make possible the administration of any provincial act by the federal Department of Labour if any province so desires.
These consultations with the provinces, management and labour organizations brought out valuable suggestions which contributed to the improvement of the initial draft of the

Industrial Relations
bill. A second draft was prepared which was introduced here during the session of 1947, and was referred to the standing committee on industrial relations. It received serious consideration. The organizations which I have already mentioned were invited to appear before the committee. They did so and submitted their considered views on the proposed legislation. The bill was redrafted and reintroduced in 1948, thoroughly examined by the committee, and finally adopted and brought into effect on September 1, 1948.
The administration of this statute has given good results so far. It would be unfair and unwise, I submit, to amend an important feature of such legislation without seeking that measure of previous consultation and concurrence with all parties concerned, and not only a few of them. The Department of Labour is not and must not become identified with the interests of one of the parties in industry to the exclusion and seemingly against the will of the other. The minister and his officials have always striven to uphold and safeguard their position as mediator between the two parties, and in their legitimate effort to hold that balance they must be inspired and assisted by legislation and regulations which have been enacted in the same spirit of impartiality as between management and labour.
If parliament were to enact the bill sponsored by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), what stand could it take if and when management organizations would attempt to obtain, by legislative action, provisions which might react against organized labour as has occurred in other countries? I should like, if I may, to cite here a few words of the late Humphrey Mitchell, which may be found in Hansard for 1947 at page 4231. He said:
. . . may I say that we have received representations for the inclusion of measures severely curtailing union activities; from others have come suggestions which would involve, under certain conditions, the compulsory application of the principle of union security in collective agreements and the adoption of other innovations.
We have not given effect in this legislation to such representations, since it is not the desire of the government to place impediments in the way of free collective bargaining between employers and their organized workers, or to legislate conditions or terms of employment that properly lie in the field of collective bargaining.
In the same speech on June 17, 1947, the late Mr. Mitchell had this to say:
Human nature cannot be corrected by a law, and in the final analysis the major consideration in improving human relations between employers and employees is the simple matter of trying to see each other's point of view and developing mutual understanding.
(Mr. Cote (Verdun-La Salle).]
There are other quotations from the same gentleman which would be of interest in discussing this subject, but I would hurry on to a reference which I should like to make to statements by my hon. friend and by others who supported him in the presentation of this amendment in years past. I refer to the debate which took place on the bill to put an end to the railway dispute which had resulted in a nation-wide strike in 1950. On August 30 the leader of the C.C.F. (Mr. Cold-well) said that the house must try to "ensure that free collective bargaining and social justice will remain fundamental parts of our Canadian way of life". The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) had this to say, as found at page 39 of Hansard of the same date:
Nevertheless the workers are fearful-and I believe they have every reason to be-that if this bill passes employers will take it as a precedent and that whenever workers make demands there will be no further bargaining in good faith because employers will expect the government to make the same provision for them.
My good friend and practically my desk-mate in the house, the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll), had this to say, as found at page 39 of Hansard for that session:
Yet this bill could be construed as saying to the trade unions that in such and such circumstances you are no longer free to exercise your rights.
Further on he said:
Neither today's government nor today's opposition in this house can undertake to say what the effect of passing this bill will be, though we say it is confined to a particular strike in 1950. There it is for all of us to see in the future. We ask ourselves the question, will it not be extended in the future by administrations less friendly to labour than our own?
As a matter of fact the hon. member for Spadina made a very thought-provoking speech on that occasion, and I should like to quote more of what he said. Further on he had this to say:
I believe it would be nothing short of a national calamity if we were to substitute something else for the collective bargaining process . . . Compulsion can force the parties to submit to a given procedure. It may even force them to accept unwillingly certain results. But I think this house knows very well that forced obedience generates resistance and hostility. Far from being a cure, it is a source of further conflict and it multiplies strife instead of preventing it. Compulsion never removes the cause of the strife.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48    VOLUNTARY REVOCABLE CHECK- OFF OF UNION DUES
speechtext:
As it is six o'clock, the hour for private and public bills has expired. At eight o'clock the house will resume consideration of the business which was interrupted at five o'clock.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.
The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. St. Laurent for the appointment of a committee to examine defence expenditures and commitments, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Claxton.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in the debate in connection with this resolution which was in the name of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent.) and introduced this afternoon by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton), which calls for a select committee to be appointed to continue the examination of all expenditure of public moneys for national defence, etc., I would first like to call attention to the fact that members on this side of the house have for many years been pressing for committees to be set up to discuss and investigate the handling of moneys which were allocated to the Department of National Defence out of the public treasury in order to provide for the essential services for the defence of this country and for the fulfilment of those obligations which Canada has undertaken in the international field.
The reason we have been pressing for the establishment of those committees was that we felt there was sufficient evidence to indicate that the taxpayers' money was not being spent to the best advantage. I remember quite clearly that in my first session in this house after I had been elected in 1945 this question of the establishment of committees was raised. I am not going back to quote from the record as far back as that, but I would just like to put on the record a statement which was made by the present leader of this party in April of 1949, when at page 2322 of Hansard these words were used:
In past years requests have been made for a select committee to examine this subject-
That is the question of national defence.
*-and to report to the house upon the basis of information of that kind. Without the delay involved in submitting any formal resolution I urge upon the government, in all earnestness and seriousness, the immediate setting up of a special select committee to examine the present state of our national defence and to make recommendations in regard to future organization and requirements.
In the year 1951, on May 8, the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness) used these words, at page 2840 of Hansard:
I think the only way we can do it at all reasonably is by means of a committee on defence. We
Committee on Defence Expenditure
have asked for such a committee every session during the past several years, and every session the minister has produced a number of what I would call excuses as to why such a committee should not be set up. I think there is no question but that this is the only way a real scrutiny of defence estimates and expenditures can be made by this House of Commons, and I would again urge the minister to set up such a committee.
In 1950 and again in 1951 I moved resolutions in this house to appoint such a committee. The wording of the resolution I moved on March 14, 1950, is to be found on page 730 of Hansard and is to this effect:
It is expedient to appoint a special committee of this house to examine and report upon the Department of National Defence and the armed services of Canada; and that such committee have power to call for persons, papers and records, and to report from time to time to this house.
Again the following year I moved a similar motion. In every case these motions were defeated by the supporters of the government casting their vote against them. Even though the committee which was set up a year ago, and the select committee which is being set up now to continue the work of that committee established a year ago were not entirely the type of committee that we were recommending in those days, I believe it is fair to say that that committee has achieved beneficial results to this country. This has been done even though the committee has found difficulty in obtaining all the information that it required, and even though at times its full endeavours, as I shall show later, have been restricted.
The main results accruing from the endeavours of this committee have been that there has developed in all service establishments across this country a general tightening up of the administration, undoubtedly due to the light of publicity which has been thrown on their system of organization and administration as a result of the researches made by this select committee. We are in favour, therefore, of establishing another select committee to continue the work which the select committee of last session started. We hope that a full opportunity will be given to that committee to investigate all the operations and expenditures of money by the defence services, as outlined in the resolution which is before us at this time.
This afternoon the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) dealt at some considerable length with the report that has been submitted by Mr. Currie, who had been asked by the minister last spring to inquire into certain alleged irregularities that it was suspected had occurred at the great camp at Petawawa, particularly in connection with the army works services. The minister read from a prepared statement of some considerable length, which took up some hour and a

Committee on Defence Expenditure half of time this afternoon. I believe that the house expected a full and complete statement, because the minister had not been present when the Currie report was tabled. He was away in Europe on government duty. I should like to make an interjection here to welcome him back to the house, and to express my pleasure that he survived the flights across the Atlantic and the other perils to which he was exposed. We welcome him back in safety and in good health. Perhaps he would not mind my saying that it might have been just as well that he was not here when the report was tabled, because I doubt very much whether we Should have gotten home for our Christmas recess.
However, the long report the minister has made requires further study, and I cannot hope to deal with it adequately this evening though I shall do my best to reply to some of the remarks he made. To begin with, he told the story of the works services and of the corps of engineers of the Canadian army. He pointed out that these works services had been reduced to very small strength a few years ago before the Korean operations started, and because they were understaffed they found that they had a tremendous amount of work to undertake. In his report Mr. Currie refers also to the same difficulties that the units of the works services experienced.
I should like to point out at this time that the reduction of those units, as well as the reduction of many other units, both fighting and administrative, was the direct result of Liberal government policy adopted a few years ago. This policy reduced these units to mere skeletons. The works services found that they were ill-equipped to play their part in providing that reasonable security which the Department of National Defence, under this government, was charged with providing in fulfilment of its obligations. It is no disgrace to the soldiers of the works services that they were few in number. I should like to emphasize the point that the reduction in the strength of these units was the direct result of the government's policy. When these units were faced with the rapid expansion which was required in order to meet the crisis which had gradually developed in Korea, they found that they had neither the equipment nor the personnel to provide that rapid expansion. These disturbances in the Far East were like the writing on the wall, and could well have been foreseen. These units, however, ran into difficulty because of the faulty government policy of those days.
Personnel had been demobilized and many of the old reliable works foremen, warrant officers, petty officers and so forth, had been


let out at the end of the war. There was difficulty in providing personnel who were trained in administration, personnel who, through years of having to stretch the very scanty funds which were provided for national defence in those days, had grown up with the psychology that the taxpayers' money must be carefully guarded and made to go as far as possible. This psychology has perhaps a great many points which the younger soldiers have not as yet appreciated.
Then because of the hasty demobilization the various training camps across the country from the Atlantic to the Pacific had been allowed to deteriorate, with some of the equipment being looted, and some camps like that at Farnham finding that huts had been completely removed.

These camps had been
allowed to fall into a state of disrepair, and so an extra burden fell largely upon the works services.
Then the minister went on to explain the table, appendix "B", which is at the end of the Currie report. He referred to a good many figures which I have not been able to study or check. In fact at one time I felt that I was almost back in school again dealing with some problem in algebra which went something like this:	If X equals 154, and Y
equals 33, then X over Y equals 15. I think those were the figures given by the minister, although he did not refer to the Y's. We shall have to inquire into those matters in further detail.
Then he went on to assure us that the Currie report had received1 consideration and that many of the recommendations had already been adopted. We forecast that possibility when this matter was under discussion before Christmas; and we can only express satisfaction that some action has already been taken on the recommendations made in the report.
To sum up that part of the minister's remarks, it would seem to me that he was once again giving us assurances that all was well. In fact, he almost appeared to be defending the army. Mr. Speaker, the army does not need any defending. It is the government which needs to be defended. It has been clearly demonstrated that, while there were opportunities for theft, fraud and dishonesty elsewhere, the army still refused to march through the door which had been left open to the would-be pilferer. No, Mr. Speaker, the army does not require any

defending. It is for the government to defend itself and to explain, how it has taken care of the $2 billion of the taxpayers' money which this department has been called upon to expend in the cause of national defence.
Last spring, as reported at page 2334 of Hansard of May 19, 1952, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) said:
Our job is to use every means possible so as to ensure that the utmost care is taken in safeguarding public property and in preventing loss, whether it be by fire, theft, fraud or any other means.
With that statement we most heartily agree, but it has to be shown that at the time the government was exercising every means it had at its disposal in order to prevent this loss through fire, theft and fraud. In the Currie report, almost at the beginning of it, when discussing the discovery of the irregularities at Petawawa Mr. Currie uses these words:
-it is an unhappy circumstance that the beginning of this investigation lies not inside the Department of National Defence and its full complement of regulations and supervising personnel, but with the receipt of an anonymous letter couched in the following terms:
Then he gives the terms of the letter which called attention to the losses and which aroused the interest of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Then Mr. Currie in his report goes on to use these words:
Before reciting the irregularities and their circumstances uncovered by the R.C.M.P.-with the assistance later of the provincial police and the army provost corps-it must be said that internal warnings had not been lacking in the Department of National Defence. The chief auditor of the department had performed his functions conscientiously. Time and again he had reported unsatisfactory conditions.
Then he goes on and refers to appendix "B" which I have already mentioned, and he closes that paragraph by saying:
Aside from reports being delayed for considerable periods of time, the record shows the next audit revealing conditions similar to those previously reported, and in some cases, worse. The process is then again repeated.
These matters have been brought to the attention of the Department of National Defence. Surely the serious implications of a report by the chief auditor of the department should have been brought to the attention of the minister and government. It is for these reasons that I feel the government is charged with the responsibility; and the government has shown that it has not taken every possible means to safeguard the taxpayers' money, in spite of the fact that in that very spring the Minister of National Defence was declaring that his job was to take care of the taxpayers' money by every possible means.
Committee on Defence Expenditure
Then the minister went on to say that nobody wished to question the report, but he himself proceeded to do so. First of all he raised the question of the horses, which has become a laughingstock and the gibe of every cartoonist across the country. He declared that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) the day before had announced that there had been no horses on the payroll. However, I could not help remarking that the Prime Minister himself based those remarks partly upon information supplied by a man who had been convicted of dishonesty and placed in a penitentiary. He seemed to prefer the statement of a criminal to that of his own appointed investigator, Mr. Currie; because Mr. Currie distinctly says there were horses on the payroll under the names of non-existent labourers. Then the minister went on to say:
There are a number of other cases in which the account given by Mr. Currie is not wholly in accordance with the facts which were established.
I do submit that Mr. Currie was sent to establish the facts. And no doubt Mr. Currie did establish those facts, even though they may not be particularly welcome facts for the government.
There is some question about a dam being built at Tucker creek at the cost of some $3,000 or $4,000. The minister explained that that was carried out as an exercise by the engineers. Well, I have no doubt that the engineers would be required to be exercised in the construction of dams. It is a fortunate fact-perhaps I should say it is a peculiar circumstance-that Tucker creek was in the centre of an area which many years ago was a favourite rendezvous of the Petawawa fish and game club.
Then the minister went on to explain about the Canadian National Railways, and the spur which Mr. Currie said had been taken up to replace the rails of the Canadian Pacific Railway spur, after the rails of the C.P.R. had been stolen, or at least after officials of that railway had protested against the sudden disappearance of those rails. The minister referred to these C.N.R. rails by saying: "I am sorry the report contained a reference to the Canadian National Railways. It turned out not to be so. I am sorry it contained a reference to the horses, though I am glad they were not on the payroll."
Regarding the C.N.R. track, there is a spur which leads from the Canadian National line into Petawawa Camp. It has been there for years and years, and everyone refers to it as the C.N.R. spur. If the rails had been laid by the government, instead of by the C.N.R., then I suppose in general terms it would be correct to say that they were not

Committee on Defence Expenditure C.N.R. rails. But tor years and years that spur has been referred to as the Canadian National spur.
Then we were admonished to view the report in its correct perspective. I do not wish to go into every detail of the report, because there is no time for that; but I think one of the general and main points in connection with what Mr. Currie found is that there was a general breakdown in the system of administration, supervision and accounting. Those are the words which are to be found very near the beginning of the report, at page 2 of the typewritten copies. It is said that this resulted in or created a generally lax administrative situation. From that Mr. Currie deduced that such a situation would give rise to waste and inefficiency far more costly in loss than that covered by the actual dishonesty.
Then, dealing with Petawawa camp itself, he referred to a small group of crooks-and they were a small group-who did take advantage of the door which the government had left open for them so they could loot and pilfer from that camp. I think the majority of hon. members know what was taken from the camp, because it has been mentioned many times in the press across the country. One need only refer to the 550 tons of so-called scrap, which included many things which were far from being scrap, such as serviceable kitchen ranges, shower stalls and the like.
Then there was a question as to lumber which had been stolen during the process of clearing large sections of the camp. Cement had been taken or had not been accounted for to the extent of some 18,000 bags. I am told that about a thousand bags of cement go to make one carload, so one might almost say that 18,000 bags would be approximately a trainload of cement which was missing altogether.
Contractors had been paid for work which had not been done, or which was completed with the loan of army equipment and personnel.
In the attempt of the government to belittle what took place-and there has been a very definite attempt on the part of the government to belittle the general breakdown in the system of administration, supervision and accounting, as reported in the Currie report -this process of belittling has taken the form of trying to refer to these very considerable losses as being relatively small matters. It is possible that they may be relatively small matters when compared with the possible losses elsewhere, in areas which have not been submitted to the scrutiny of Mr. Currie and his team of accountants,


because Mr. Currie's endeavours were limited to the relatively small field of the army works services, mainly at Petawawa camp, though he did investigate and did find some irregularities in other camps serviced by the army works services.
These are not relatively small matters if viewed in regard to the actual loss of taxpayers' money, and the lowering of morale that has been caused by all these losses, through the light of publicity that has been thrown upon them. When Mr. Currie was first appointed the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) said:
We felt that no better man could be found to do this job if we searched the length and breadth of the country.
Then he went on to point out that Mr. Currie was an ex-officer who had served during the first world war with distinction, that he had been a deputy minister of the Department of National Defence for a number of years, and that he was also a member of a very prominent firm of chartered accountants. It is certain that nobody on this side of the house, or anywhere in the house, disputed the fact at that time that Mr. Currie appeared to have all the qualifications which were necessary to carry out such an investigation. Now we are asking ourselves, why has Mr. Currie fallen from grace; because it is quite obvious that in their endeavour to play down and belittle his report they have not stopped even at casting reflections upon Mr. Currie himself. I wonder whether, when they made the appointment, they overlooked the fact that Mr. Currie, besides his qualifications as an ex-officer, a deputy minister of national defence and a chartered accountant, was also an honourable and honest gentleman.
I said that an attempt was being made to belittle this report. It started when the Solicitor General (Mr. Campney) replied just before Christmas. In referring to quotations which have been made from the report by hon. members on this side of the house he described them as exaggerations, as irresponsible statements. Then last week on Vancouver island the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) referred to the Currie report merely as "threshing old straw." On Vancouver island the Solicitor General also referred to the report and said that it would not "cut much ice." The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) was a little more emphatic, and when speaking at Kingston he is reported as having said that "it was a rehash in lurid language" of matters already dealt with by the courts or by the department.
I have read out some extracts from this report. It has been made available to every hon. member; it has been published in the

papers. I defy any hon. member to point to any lurid language which is used in the report. The report is written in the most moderate terms, but it has stated honestly and exactly what the conditions were as they were found by Mr. Currie when he was making his investigation. Even though the Solicitor General may laugh, I think he will find it very difficult, with his knowledge of the English language and the meaning of words, to point to any sentences which really can answer to the description of being lurid in language.
Well, after drawing attention to these irregularities and to the losses which had been sustained at Petawawa camp, Mr. Currie draws various conclusions and makes these observations:	Although the Department of
National Defence auditors were warned again and again over a lengthy period that supervision and accounting were inadequate, no effective action was ever taken, with the result the situation grew progressively worse and the discovery of thefts, following investigation, came not from the department itself but from an anonymous letter to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police; and again:
No reliable estimate of the total loss can be prepared. . . How many more there may have been will never be known.
And again:
There was, in addition, a serious collapse in security. There was little to prevent or to detect the organized plundering of military stores on a systematic scale. . . If there is excuse for inefficient accounting, there is none for the failure of security which is, after all, a prime military consideration. I take a serious view of this breakdown.
Perhaps the Solicitor General considers that lurid language. I do not know. I do not think it would answer the description of the word "lurid" as given in the Oxford dictionary, or in any other reliable dictionary.
Then there is a paragraph which has been quoted before in this house, and which is found on page 17 of the report, which summarizes the conditions to which I have already referred this evening. These are the lurid words of the framer of this report, Mr. Currie:
The situation was complicated by still another factor. The Department of National Defence (including the army works services) was largely staffed and manned by men whose military training had been received in wartime. Its establishment and administrative practices reflected more clearly the urgent needs and exigencies of war, when speed is everything and costs count not at all.
That is again the direct result of government policy. The government had seen fit to remove many of the more senior, perhaps more elderly, staff officers of 1946-1947, and they had been replaced very largely by the younger commanders who had quite naturally 68108-61J
Committee on Defence Expenditure grown up in this war psychology. I remember pointing out at the time the dangers of this policy. I made this statement in this house on the 6th day of February, 1947, when speaking in the debate on national defence, as reported at page 173 of Hansard:
I suggest that all the substance has been taken out of our defence force and that today there remains only the wreckage of the overhead framework.
In those days the government had reduced the services to such a state that they were not in an efficient position to carry out their responsibilities. And even in those days attention had been called by the Auditor General, and by the auditors of the department as well, to the unsatisfactory accounting conditions which had existed. At the same time we were receiving solemn assurances that all was well, and that there were no irregularities or deficiencies in the various construction projects at Petawawa camp. Mr. Currie shortly afterward was carrying out his investigation, and he was reporting that there were unauthorized projects, that there were improper loans of material and that the rental of army equipment was taking place to civilian contractors.
In the recently published Auditor General's report for last year these irregularities are confirmed, and other cases have been cited that deal not only with Petawawa camp but with other army establishments throughout the country. He complains of the complicated accounting system which has prevented losses from being reported and brought to the attention of those responsible for the safeguarding of the taxpayers' money. I might cite as an example of that the mixing of gas and fuel oil at Churchill which, according to Mr. Sellar, seems to have cost the taxpayers somewhere in the neighbourhood of $75,000 or $80,000.
I do suggest that if the government were really determined to safeguard the taxpayers' money it would not have adopted the policy of belittling the Currie report. I think it is one of the tragedies of this whole unfortunate episode that the government should have adopted the attitude of ridiculing and belittling the report. It would have been far more seemly if they had swallowed the pill and decided that they would investigate the conditions thoroughly. It would have been far more seemly if they had, with a contrite heart, accepted all the recommendations made by Mr. Currie. It is a pill that they must swallow. It may be an unpleasant one, but unless all the ingredients of the pill are taken we shall never get the patient well again.

They are choking on it now.

Committee on Defence Expenditure

It was proposed by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) this afternoon, and was also mentioned by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), that the report would be referred to the select committee which is now to be set up. I suggest that it is action that is required, and not the referring of the report to a committee. We might well examine the constitution of the select committee to be set up to continue the work of last year's committee. It is to consist of some 26 members. According to the constitution of the committee last year, 17 of its 26 members were members or supporters of the government. In other words, 17 out of 26 were Liberals. Six were drawn from the ranks of the Progressive Conservative party and three from all other groups in the house. Therefore if the representatives of the Conservatives and the other groups all voted together they were only able to marshal 9 votes against the 17 of the supporters of the government on the committee.
I do not think it is going too far to say that the committee was really a one-party organization. If members from the opposition groups wished to find out about certain matters and it was not the wish of the government that details along those particular lines should be revealed then these matters were a closed book to the committee. It was suggested that the committee should take up the question of Petawawa camp. That was refused. It was said that we must not go into the matter of Petawawa camp because the Currie commission was investigating it. There was some question about making inquiries regarding item No. 87(a) on a list provided for us, which item dealt with aircraft for the R.C.A.F. and the navy. One would think that a defence expenditures committee would be permitted to investigate the expenditure of a sum which at that time was listed at no less than $668,986,840, of which over $100 million was to be spent in that year. But no; the committee must not investigate any spending in connection with such a large sum of money as $668 million odd.
Obviously when the government does not like its actions to be queried it finds means in that committee and elsewhere to limit the investigations which the committee would like to carry out and the disclosure of information which should be brought to attention elsewhere. It is fairly obvious that no sooner had the Auditor General's report been tabled than officials of the Department of National Defence, unnamed of course, rushed into print and started to comment upon the remarks made by the Auditor General. This department is following the pattern set up by the government. It is resentful of any criticism


which may be offered of it. We are uncertain whether the committee now to be appointed will be able under the circumstances to carry out the duties that have been assigned to it. Immediately after the house rose for the Christmas recess the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) communicated with the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent).
Order. I hesitate to interrupt the hon. member, but it does occur to me that he is coming close to questioning the independence of the members of the committee.
Oh, oh.
He has not gone quite to that extreme, but he is close to it. There is a rule of the house that every member is an independent member.
They are the only honest members.
Order. I felt that I should bring the rule to the attention of hon. members at this time.
Let us be careful not to hurt anybody's feelings.

Mr. Speaker, when you rose to point out that you thought that I might be questioning the independence of members I was about to read a letter written by the Leader of the Opposition to the Prime Minister just before Christmas. I have the permission of the Leader of the Opposition to read it. In fact I think the letter has been published, and I do not think you will find anything in it that questions the independence of any member of the house, myself or anybody else. These are the words which were used in the letter:
You said that the Currie report would be submitted to the committee on defence expenditures. One of my reasons for writing this letter is to point out that this procedure is neither necessary nor desirable. Members of the opposition who sat on the committee made a determined effort last spring to inquire into the situation at Petawawa. They were denied any opportunity to do so with the explanation that this might prejudice the trials of those already charged with theft, and also that Mr. Currie had been appointed to conduct an inquiry, which would deal fully with that situation.
We need no inquiry into the report of another inquiry. We need action on the report now before us. It makes positive recommendations. You have expressed your confidence in Mr. Currie's integrity, ability and good judgment. We share that confidence in every respect. I submit that it is the duty of the government to act on those recommendations without delay. I further submit that it is the duty of the government to conduct a similar inquiry into every aspect of the organization and administration of the Department of National Defence. I repeat my request that Mr. Currie be given this authority.

Now, if those words were pertinent, as they were before Christmas, they are very definitely underlined now that the Auditor General's report has been received. We fear, as we have said before, that the defence expenditures committee may not be able to go into all the details of operations and expenditures of money that it would like to go into. Petawawa camp has been cited as one case and it is possible that the committee, in its final report or in its actions which will produce that final report, will reflect the will of the government rather than the rights of the citizens because, whether we would like to feel we can be independent or not, we do know that there is party discipline and that it is such that the government can rely upon the majority of its supporters to support it in anything it does. In fact, I would go so far as to say that in some respects we have travelled a long way on the road to Moscow and that we do live on the edge of a dictatorship.
Hear, hear.
It is the return trip that is tough.

In case the committee cannot fulfil all the functions that it would like to fulfil or that it is called upon to fulfil by the Prime Minister's resolution, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness), a further amendment which reads as follows:
(a)	By striking out the words of the amendment, namely: "and initially to give priority in their examination to the expenditures and commitments of the Canadian army works services as dealt with in the report of G. S. Currie, Esquire, chartered accountant, tabled in the House of Commons on December 15, 1952", and,
(b)	by adding at the end of the motion as amended the following words:
"and inasmuch as the report of G. S. Currie on the Department of National Defence is a matter of prime importance to the people of Canada this house is of the opinion that the said G. S. Currie should be authorized to continue his inquiries and conduct a similar investigation to that already undertaken into all aspects of organization, accounting and administration of the Department of National Defence."

I was starting to give my
ruling.

May I say a word with respect to that, sir? The amendment which was offered this afternoon by a minister of the crown to a government motion, proposes that certain instructions be given to the committee with reference to the Currie report. TMr. St. Laurent.]

Now, with respect, Mr. Speaker, that is not an expanded negative. In order to come within the rule the Prime Minister is invoking it has to be an expanded negative and nothing more. This is a great deal more. This deals with the same subject matter, and with great respect I submit that on the first point the Prime Minister's objection is not well taken.
On the second point, sir, the Prime Minister raises the ground that this is a new subject matter that is introduced. If it means that this amendment to the amendment is to be ruled out now by this appeal of the Prime Minister to subtlety, I think it will be clear to the house and the public just why it was that a government minister this afternoon introduced this amendment to a government motion.

As I said this afternoon, I cannot be concerned with what the effect of either allowing or disallowing an amendment will be. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I say that with all due apologies to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson). At any rate, Mr. Speaker, we hope that this committee will be able to make inquiries that will be useful, and that some progress will be made in tightening up the administration-and in particular the financial administration-of the Department of National Defence.
Likewise we have no quarrel with the substance of the amendment moved this afternoon by the Minister of National Defence, which suggests that the defence expenditure committee should give priority to consideration of the Currie report. In saying this we have no illusions as to what is likely to happen. We are satisfied that there will be an attempt by the government members of that *committee to whitewash that report. Nevertheless, in our view the report stands on its own feet and an attempt to whitewash it, though it may be done by a majority vote, will not be effective or successful in the eyes of the Canadian people who have been shocked at the disclosures which have come about as a result of the investigation made by Mr. Currie.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that in our view the speech of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton)

Committee on Defence Expenditure this afternoon, while it covered a great many aspects of the matter now before us, was one in which he completely overlooked what to us is one of the most serious aspects of this whole question. Not only did he, in our view, overlook what we regard as of serious concern, but he made comments which seemed to me to suggest that he would not appreciate the seriousness of the point even if it were drawn to his attention. The point that we feel is most serious about this whole business is the question as to the proper place of the armed forces in a democracy. Are they the servant of the state, of the people of the country through their elected representatives, or are they in charge? Are the armed forces entitled to dictate to the government and to push other people around? In our view there has been too much evidence of that attitude throughout this whole business, and that is our primary concern at the present time.
I may say, Mr. Speaker, that during the last month several things have happened which have underlined our concern as to who is running the show, the heads of the army or the elected government of this country. Our first concern over that matter arose on the morning of December 15 when the Prime Minister tabled the official copy of the Currie report. Hon. members will recall that, when he tabled the report, he placed on Hansard at the same time a memorandum from the chief of the general staff. During the course of his remarks at that time he stated that he was giving us that memorandum because the chief of the general staff thought that the views contained in that memorandum should be given publicity at the same time as the revelations contained in the Currie report itself. When the Prime Minister was questioned by my deskmate, the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright), during the course of debate in the next day or so as to why he had done this, the Prime Minister interjected to say that he was prepared to give the answer right then and there. He said he did it because he was requested to do so by the chief of the general staff. In our view, Mr. Speaker, the chief of the general staff had no right to ask the elected Prime Minister of this country to table that memorandum, and in our view the Prime Minister had no right to accede to that request. We take a strong view of that whole incident as indicative of a state of mind on the part of the top officers in the army which is not consistent with democratic practice.
It should be made clear, Mr. Speaker, that though what we say seems to be by way of levelling blame at the chief of the general staff, it should not be forgotten that it is the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton), it is the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent),

it is the government which is responsible for the kind of set-up that they have in the general staff, responsible for the attitude that the heads of the army display in a situation like this. They have to take the responsibility for it; and as the heads of a democratic state I submit that they are missing the whole point.
Now, that was the first evidence in this present story of the domineering attitude on the part of the military staff. The second evidence, in our view, was the fact that a draft of Mr. Currie's report was shown to the deputy minister of national defence, and perhaps was seen by others, with the result that suggestions were made as to changes that might be made in that report.
I shall have something to say a little later about the fact that a copy of the first draft of this report came into the possession of my leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). But let it be made clear right now that no one doubts the authenticity of this draft which my leader received, and no one denies that changes were made.
Between the first draft and the second draft changes were made. For instance, on page 17 the words "at or near the top" were deleted and in their place were put the words "higher up".
The Prime Minister confirmed on Wednesday, December 17, that a copy of the first draft of the report had been given to the deputy minister of national defence, and that at least one other official in the department had seen it. When I asked whether the chief of the general staff had seen it, he said that he did not know. This afternoon the Minister of National Defence likewise confirmed the fact that that first draft of the report was placed in the hands of the deputy minister. And we learned one further item this afternoon from the minister, namely that prior to that first copy of the report in multilith, there was a typewritten copy showing the form in which the report was to be set up, and that that, too, had been shown to the deputy minister.
The Minister of National Defence said this afternoon that he could not understand why we were at all concerned about the fact that the earlier draft, or earlier drafts, were shown to the deputy minister. He made great play on the fact that it was he who had appointed Mr. Currie, and that it was his desire and wish that there should be this report.
I suggest to the Minister of National Defence that what this parliament and this country thought when Mr. Currie was appointed to do this job was that we would get a completely independent report-and I

hope I can still use the word "independent" in this house. We had hoped it would be a completely independent report, objective and without any influence being brought to bear on the investigator by those being investigated.
Now, how anyone can imagine that there would be a complete lack of such influence, when earlier drafts of that report were taken to the people being investigated, is beyond my power to understand. The Minister of National Defence, although he is the minister and thus the head of the department and responsible for it, seems to partake of the attitude of his top officials and officers, because he told us this afternoon that when Mr. Currie objected to showing Mr. Drury the first copy-the first multilith copy-he, the Minister of National Defence, suggested to his deputy minister that further conversation be had about this, and that perhaps Mr. Currie could be persuaded to let a copy of his report in that form be seen by the department.
In other words, the Minister of National Defence is part and parcel with his military heads, and all the rest of them, in this feeling that in connection with any investigation that is being made into the affairs of that department, any report to be made upon the basis of that investigation can be seen by them before that report is put in its final form and presented to the minister for presentation to parliament.
In other words, along with the earlier incident to which I referred, here you have what to me is proof positive of the fact that in the military heads of this country today we have this feeling, that somehow or another it is their show, that they have the right to say what is to be done, that they have the right to run it, rather than it being the right of the elected people, or of the government chosen by the people of this country.
Mr. Speaker, to us this is a matter of principle which is extremely important, and we feel that this government has been in power so long that it has forgotten some of the basic principles of democracy. It has forgotten the relationship that should exist between the government of a democracy and the armed forces.
You sure have forgotten the principle.

Now, after that part of the story, the next item which was of interest to me was to read in the press a day or two after we left here for the Christmas recess that the same chief of the general staff- and if I mention his name repeatedly, I 68108-62
