Indeed as I have said, I was amazed to read in the press that the chief of the general staff had issued orders that members of the armed forces and employees of the Department of National Defence were requested not to discuss the Currie report. Well, Mr. Speaker, the more these things come to light, the more one wonders just how well those on the government benches understand the meaning of democracy. Surely it is inconceivable that employees of the Department of National Defence and, in fact, people in uniform, should be denied the right to discuss the Currie report. Well, it is inconceivable; but we have had so many displays of this arrogant and domineering attitude on the part of the top military people who do not seem to realize that this is a democracy, that perhaps it is all of a piece that they seek to deny the right to free discussion.
But while the chief of the general staff denies to the people to whom he can issue orders the right to discuss the Currie report, he does not hesitate to discuss it himself. One need only mention the memorandum he requested the Prime Minister to table on December 15, when the Currie report was first tabled. But there is now before us the December issue of the Canadian Army Journal. This issue is dated December, 1952, but apparently it came out only within the last day or two. So far as I can ascertain it made its appearance only yesterday.
I find on pages 2 and 3 of this issue a message to the Canadian army from the chief of the general staff. It is over the signature of G. G. Simonds, lieutenant-general, and chief of the general staff. Hon. members are aware of what is in this message, because it has been given wide publicity in the press of today. It is a very nicely worded document. It does not say members of parliament have been saying some things they should not have said, but the reference is very clearly to the discussions which have gone on in this House of Commons. It says, for example:
In recent weeks and months the army has been the target of unremitting attacks from many sources. We have been criticized for the indiscipline of Canadian soldiers. We have been criticized for too much discipline. We have been criticized for extravagance and criticized for not providing a whole host of things which cost a very great deal of money. We have been criticized for lack of morale and accused of complacency and arrogance when we have shown or proclaimed a pride in the Canadian army.

Committee on Defence Expenditure
Then he goes on, after a few more sentences, to say:
Some of this criticism has been, and will continue to be, unfairly biased and irresponsible-
That is what the chief of general staff is saying about what members of parliament, in discharging their responsibilities to their constituents, have been saying here in the House of Commons. He says:
Some of this criticism has been, and will continue to be, unfairly biased and irresponsible but that will be as clear to the citizens and taxpayers outside the army as to those that serve in it.
Perhaps it would not have been quite so bad for the chief of general staff to take to himself the right to make these comments about discussions that have taken place in parliament, if he had not already been responsible for an order requesting those to whom he can issue orders not to discuss the Currie report. The concluding sentence in this message from the chief of the general staff reads:
I charge every soldier to apply himself in all those matters where we clearly need improvement but not to be discouraged or depressed by criticisms which are neither founded on truth nor justified in the light of our positive achievements.
Whose criticism is he referring to as neither founded on truth nor justified? The criticisms made in this House of Commons; the criticisms made by Mr. Currie? Apparently it is both. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that it is high time the minister, who accepts responsibility for all that goes on in the armed forces, took a look at this kind of thing and asked the question as to where it fits into the whole concept of democracy under which, in our view, the armed forces should be the servants and not the masters of the state.
Well, still another bit of evidence of this attitude has already been referred to by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) who took his seat only a few moments ago. As hon. members know, there appeared yesterday the public accounts and the Auditor General's report for the year ending March 31, 1952. In this report there are a number of references to things that had been happening in the financial administration of the armed forces. There is reference to a brigadier who for three months was drawing two government pay cheques, one for his service as a civil servant seconded to duties here in Ottawa and one for his rank in the army. There is reference to an area commandant who had something to do with having a house improved to the extent of $15,000, when the amount approved for those improvements was only $800; and incidentally, it comes out now in the press at any rate that that particular person was

Brigadier Connelly who was recently retired, and we in this house were not given at that time the information as to why he was retired. It raises another question. Why was this brigadier posted to Tokyo, if it was after the disclosures contained in the Auditor General's report with respect to his part in going beyond the financial regulations under which the Department of National Defence is supposed to function?
The Minister of National Defence said clearly, and I was not surprised-I would expect him to say what he said this afternoon, in view of his academic knowledge of democracy-that he is responsible for what goes on. Well, he is responsible for this. Immediately we get the tabling of Mr. Watson Sellar's report we get a blast from the officials of the Department of National Defence against Mr. Watson Sellar. Well, it is not the first time that the Auditor General has been criticized. When the same people who have been taking this attitude in all of the instances I have indicated here, again take that attitude today in the light of Mr. Watson Sellar's report, that is a clear indication that we have to check this kind of thing and ask the question whether or not the general staff of our army is getting out of hand and seeking to run the show which should be run by the democratically elected people of this country.

Dear Mr. Minister,
With further reference to your letter of the 22nd December and my acknowledgment thereof dated 24th December, I now give you further particulars in regard to the print reproduction and submission of my report.
Some time prior to the completion of my report in the form to have it print reproduced, I asked my partner, Mr. Davey, to call upon the deputy minister of national defence and to tell him that I did not propose to show him a copy of my draft report. On the 5th November 1952 Mr. Davey called upon the deputy minister of national defence and told him that, notwithstanding our exchange of factual data from time to time for purposes of verification, I had no intention of submitting a draft of the report in final form prior to the actual signing and delivery of the report itself. Mr. Davey reported that the deputy minister agreed they should not see any draft report.
On the 19th November there was delivered to the printer in Montreal (later referred to) a typescript of my report for the purposes of print reproduction thereof. On the 25th November two print reproductions of my report were delivered by the printer to my office for checking and final consideration. Under the offset print reproduction process used by the printer, it is the practice to run off all copies required to complete the anticipated final full order, which in this case was one hundred copies. This he did, but only ten (10) copies were actually assembled as units, of which two (2) were delivered to my office as already stated, and the other eight (8) stayed with the printer and were at all times so kept and were there when the final prints (with all changes and/or additions) were required by me. If changes or additions
are necessary, the pages involved are reproduced in their entirety. I had promised that the report would be delivered to you on or before 30th November, and, had not the delay occurred through sending a copy to Ottawa, I feel I would have been able to sign the report on the 26th November. This accounts for the final report being dated 26th November.
On the 26th November before the checking and final consideration had been completed by me here, Mr. Drury, the deputy minister, called on the telephone from Ottawa. During his telephone conversation with me, Mr. Drury mentioned the minister and went on to intimate to me that it seemed desirable that the final text of the intended report be submitted to him (before the report was actually signed and delivered) in order that purely factual matters dealt with in the report could be verified as to their accuracy. I gather that his reason for this was that in such connection there had been instances in the Mainguy report where purely factual matters of this nature had not been properly dealt with. While, during this conversation with Mr. Drury, I expressed some disinclination to follow such a course, the upshot was that it was understood that I would submit to him one of the two print reproduction copies above referred to but solely for the purpose of enabling verification of factual matters and data dealt with in the report as so formulated. I decided that I would ask my partner, Mr. Cleary, to personally deliver the said copy to the deputy minister. I called Mr. Cleary, who was in Ottawa, and described the situation to him. That afternoon I had one of the two print reproduction copies which I had received from the printer mailed to Mr. Cleary, who, on the following day, the 27th November, delivered it in person to the deputy minister.
The printer already referred to has been in business in Montreal for many years and enjoys a reputation of meticulous care in maintaining the confidential nature of his business. This I had ascertained from sources which I considered reliable, before entrusting the work to him. I have attended at his office and plant and have examined the manner in which he handles his business, and I cannot believe that the copy in the hands of unauthorized third parties could have been obtained from him.
I am most anxious that this matter should be cleared up as soon as possible. If I could have an opportunity of examining the copy referred to by Mr. Knowles as being in the possession of his leader, I feel there are certain characteristics peculiar to the first print reproduction copies received from the printer which would enable me to determine

whether the copy in the possession of Mr. Knowles or his leader could, in fact, have emanated from that source. Failing being given an opportunity to examine this copy, I would welcome an investigation by some competent authority as to the origin of this mysterious copy.
Yours sincerely,
G. S. Currie.

Dear Mr. Minister,
I have your letter of the 2nd instant.
In reply to the specific questions which, as you say, naturally arise the answers which result from my detailed investigation here are as follows:
You are correct in understanding that all the ten copies that were put together have been accounted for.
As regards the further 90 unassembled prints of each page

to be used eventually to make up the 100 complete copies (as per order) I have ascertained as a result of detailed inquiries in the printer's establish-

ment that it is impossible to account for an even 90 of such prints. The reason is that, as per the printer's usual practice, they make some over-run to allow for defects or spoilage in any of the pages or sheets of the order; and in the circumstances I have found it impossible to have them account for each so created sheet or page which might be put to make up a complete copy.
The observations above made cover your third question as to whether the printer has been able to satisfy me that no other copies were made.
As you are aware, my representatives had an opportunity yesterday afternoon of seeing in Ottawa the mysterious extra copy. Having regard to its physical attributes and characteristics there appears to be no doubt that this copy is one of the first offset prints made in the printer's shop here; and I have today so informed the printer. How it got from the printer's shop into the hands of unauthorized third parties is still a complete mystery.
Everything which I have done by way of inquiry and investigation negatives the possibility that the copy in question could have got out in any stage or step between the printer's shop and my own organization and the department; but I still, of course, welcome any further investigation which the department or any other authority may deem it expedient to make from any angle or direction.
Yours sincerely,
G. S. Currie

Dear Mr. Claxton:
Thank you for your letter of January 8 and for your kind words wishing me a speedy recovery.
I have been making satisfactory progress since my recent operation and expect to be out of the hospital very shortly. I regret, however, that I shall be unable to return to my regular duties for some time.
With regard to the copy of the Currie report in my possession, I cannot disclose the name of the person who gave me this report without betraying the confidence and trust he has seen fit to place in me.
I believe that I have the right, indeed, a duty, as a member of parliament, to place before the house a matter pertaining to the public interest. I think that you will agree with me that I could not have carried out this duty if I had felt obligated to reveal the identity of the person who handed me the report. Indeed, for me to divulge this information now would have the effect of deterring members of parliament in the future from bringing to the attention of the house matters in the public interest because they were not in a position to disclose the source of their information.
